I wish to draw the attention of the minister to the large number of men in this service who are in receipt of very small salaries, the minimum amount being
under $1,200. I am speaking particularly of the men in the customs service in the city of Toronto. In view of the very large contribution, amounting to about 60 millions of dollars per annum which the port of Toronto contributes towards customs revenues, surely the men in the service there are entitled to greater consideration than they now receive. A large number of these men are returned soldiers and married, who have been in the service for years, and yet they are paid such a small amount as $1,200 a year. Surely the important work which these men are doing entitles them to receive a better salary than that. Officials in the provincial and municipal service who are doing work of a similar nature to that of these federal officials are much better paid. I earnestly hope that the minister will be able to give these poorly paid and highly deserving men a better salary than they now enjoy.

The question of salaries is
now before the Civil Service Commission for revision. I might tell my hon. friend that ever since I have been Minister of Customs I have tried to improve the status of these low-salaried men. For example I have endeavoured to obtain for them the same advantage that is enjoyed by officials in receipt of higher salaries, namely, that they should get an increase of $120 a year instead of merely $60. I was influenced in that course by the fact that the post office officials were getting that treatment on the ground that they were brought more closely into contact with the public than the officers of other departments. I have always maintained that there snould be no difference in this respect between the officers of the Post Office Department and the Customs, and that the employees of both departments who are in receipt of similar salaries should get the yearly increase of $120. I hope that when the matter comes before the Civil Service Commission I shall be able to impress them with the fact that they ought to make the $120 increase per year applicable to the customs officials, to the lower paid customs officials, the same as in the department of the postal service.

If the minister thinks
there is a discrimination in favour of the postal employees, why has the government submitted the question in regard to the postal
employees' claim first for consideration?

They were the first to
raise the question and ask for the increase.
Supply-Customs
The minister was a little slow in not bringing his much-injured employees before the commission first, when they were treated worse than the postal employees.

Two years ago the deputy minister, myself, and the officers of the department went before the commission and endeavoured to impress upon them the fact that they ought to make the recommendation that the customs officials should get the $120 increase. We did not make any public demonstration, but I thought the case was good enough to stand on its merits, and that it deserved the consideration of the Civil Service Commission when presented by the officers of the department and myself.

In what form was the
post office case presented? I understand it was presented by an order in council from the entire government-a special reference.

It was presented along with the others. I do not know the form it took; but, as far as the Customs department is concerned, I can give my hon. friend an answer. During the last two years the commissioner, the assistant commissioner and myself went to the Civil Service Commission in order to have this matter arranged.

And how is the case of the post office officials now? I understand it is dancing around between the commission and some board, deputy ministers and so forth, that it is a matter of backing and filling, and that there is no result. What is the reason there is no result in that case? Is the minister to wait until all these convolutions are completed in the case of the post office employees before doing anything?

My case stands on its
merits. I have nothing to do with the post office. I put my case before the commission, and am still pressing it, and will continue to press it until I bring it to a favourable issue.
I do not like the continual blaming of the commission.
I am not doing that.

Inferentially that is the attitude of one minister after another. They would be great men if it were not for that commission. I draw to their attention the fact that in the United' States they have by statute increased the salaries this year over the whole range, although they have a commission. If this government really believes what it is talking about, that the

commission is obstinate to-day, and if the ministers desire to be extremely generous, and if they would pay everybody well but for the commission, why do they not do as the United States government did, namely come down here with a statute that would represent their views and discharge their responsibility, instead of shunting it all the time on somebody else?

This is not a question
of increase, if you will permit me,-it is in one way, because it is a statutory increase. The law provides that officers within a certain range of salary shall get an increase of $60 a year. That refers to the lower-class officials, and I want them to get the $120 increase.

I expect it is the case
of every minister wanting something for his own, that is quite natural; but no matter what the fact is, if the government is wanting this change or that change, all they have to do is come down and do it, if they think they are not getting fair play. Why should they always be loading it on to the commission?

We are not doing that.
We are following the ordinary process.

That post office increase was referred to the commission, and it has never got back yet-at least we have had no report in regard to it. If the government believes it has a good case, and that it is not receiving right treatment from the commission, and if the minister believes that, let him come down and place his case in the form of a statute, as was done in the United States this year.
How does the minister justify the increase of salary of the Commissioner of Customs and Excise from $6,000 to $8,000? This will be found on page 83.

Last year the salaries of deputy ministers were increased from $6,000 to $8,000. That increase was given to those who had been ten years in the position- not ten years in the service. I am sorry the commissioner is here, because I would like to say a few things to the House about him. If I had my own way I would pay him $12,000, and I think I would be under-paying him then, because I think he does more for the country and more in the interests of all concerned in this country than a great many men who are receiving a bigger salary. The reason is that the government thought there would be an increase for the deputy min-

Supply-Customs
isters. Last year the Commissioner of Customs, not having been commissioner for ten years-but having been in the service forty-two years-did not qualify, under a technicality. We thought it was an injustice to the commissioner, and that the injustice should be removed, and that he should be put on the same basis as the others. I think time in the service should count, as well as time in the office. That is the reason of the increase this year.
I rise to support the minister in this particular instance. I always support him when he is right, and I wish I could do so oftener.
My hon. friend should get up every time I speak, because I am always right.

Last year I objected to the manner in which increases were being made. They were not made having regard to merit, but having regard to length of tenure of office. One of the objections I took to the general increase last year, which I think was given at the wrong time, was that the Commissioner of Customs was not included in the increase. When others were getting it, he certainly should have got it.

Customs and Excise-salaries and contingent expenses of the several ports in the Dominion, including pay for overtime of officers, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act,-and temporary buildings and rentals, $5,720,710.

How much of
this is for salaries and how much for contingencies?
The estimated salaries for the full year for the various provinces are $4,918,110, and the rest of the item is contingencies. My hon. friend tan subtract one from the other.
What is covered under the heading " Contingencies."

That covers what I call
the overhead, outside of salaries-administration of the office, light, rent, postage, express, telegrams, telephones, also to pay for overtime services of certain officers who have to work after regular hours.

Part of this item relates to temporary buildings and rentals. In this connection, what has been done to provide customs facilities for the port of Toronto from which the government is collecting between $55,000,000 and $60,000,000 a year? We have a number of old rented buildings
there and there is a great waste of money and time. A proper customs building should be erected for this important city. We are using the old station, the new union station, a large property out Wellington street, the old post office, the new post office and many other makeshift places. I understand the minister has been most active in this connection and is desirous of doing something for this particular port. Some years ago land was bought for the extension of the custom house, and during the war the old custom house on Front street was torn down. A large piece of property on the south side of Front street was bought from the city of Toronto at considerable cost, this lot to be used for the erection of a bigger and more convenient place where the citizens of Toronto could go and pay the 19^ per cent which they pay of the whole amount of excise and customs duties collected in Canada. Those who have any business to do in the custom house- wholesale men, retail men,-are battered from pillar to post with consequent loss of their time, loss of time of the staff, loss of money and many other inconveniences. From the day the old customs building was tom down to this not a dollar has ever been voted by this parliament to provide Toronto with a proper custom house. The old building which was torn down was suitable for a port with a population of only 50,000 people. Three quarters of a million people in Toronto are making use of the customs offices, and without proper transportation facilities they have to go across a territory covering between twelve and fourteen miles. When you compare the facilities provided by the late government with those provided by the present government as regards the port of Toronto, according to the venerable Globe, enough has been said to show that federal governments, whatever their complexion, not only treat Toronto as a milch cow, but refuse to provide even a stable in which to milk her,- and Toronto is becoming very impatient. The board of trade, the municipal government, the ratepayers' association, the trades and labour council and the people generally who are doing business, complain that hour after hour and day after day are wasted in trying to find just the place in which to transact business. If a merchant has some goods coming through the customs, it takes him the best part of a day to find out what building the goods are in before he can get them out. While the minister is in charge of one of the most efficient governmental departments as regards the officials and the rank and file, the buildings are not suitable,
Supply-Customs

they are ramshackle buildings and they do not conform with the municipal bylaws. The revenue collected at Toronto increases in an average by three to three and one-half million dollars ever year. We had a promise last year, and one the year before; we had a promise for about five or six years by the Union government that something was going to be done to give Toronto proper custom facilities.
The postal receipts amount to nearly $6,000,000 a year and yet Toronto cannot get a suitable post office. We have a post office that was built when Toronto had a population of
50.000	people, and now the population is about
750.000	people. If the government is getting all this revenue out of the city of Toronto, surely it would be good business to put up proper buildings. We have a very active minister and I do not like to raise difficulties, because my wish is that he get through his estimates quickly. But I hope something will be done by the government and especially the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) to remedy this grievous situation in which Toronto is placed.

It was not necessary for
my hon. friend to express the wish he did towards me to gain my sympathy for a custom house at Toronto. I agree with what he says and if they will delegate to me the power and authority to build the custom house, it will be built very quickly. The facilities in Toronto, I admit, are not adequate. The old custom house was torn down -I do not know what for. Part of the back of the old custom house is used now as an examining warehouse and you have to go to another place if you want to visit the long room. I certainly am in favour of putting up a proper building in Toronto, because Toronto deserves it on account of, not only the amount of revenue that is collected in that city, but its importance and also the service it ought to receive. I do not think it is fair for any minister or any chief of staff or inspector of a department to require full efficiency from his staff if they have not the proper quarters to work in. Not only are the public inconvenienced in Toronto by the fact that we have to trot to the station to the old custom house, and then to buildings on Wellington street and some other streets in order to get things through, but the officers are also inconvenienced because they have not the proper quarters to work in. Toronto is not the only place that is in this situation. Montreal has not proper custom house accommodation. An examining warehouse was 	*
built. The foundation was put down for a long room; the foundations are there going to waste, and the examining warehouse is being used as a long room. Another place that needs better accommodation, a place that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) must know something about, is Winnipeg. I think the Winnipeg custom house is not a fit place to put men to work in. There is no custom house in which so many applications on account of sickness are reported as Winnipeg. And this is not surprising. I have been through that custom house; it is not properly ventilated, and is not a place where men can work efficiently. As regards the construction of good buildings, especially for custom houses -and I think the Customs department and the custom houses ought to get some consideration-I may say to my colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King): After all, we give you the revenue we collect from the whole country and the people who are engaged in that work have not the most pleasant job of all. We all know what it is to ask a man for money or to take money out of a man. The smile is longer and broader when you open a letter with a cheque in it than when you open one enclosing a bill. That is human nature, and you cannot change it. Those men are working under a constant strain, and he who pays allways believes that he is paying too much, especially in connection with taxes. When you buy a cigar and pay for it, that is not as big a sacrifice as giving a dime or a dollar for something you do not see and you do not know what you are getting for your money. As regards municipal taxes, there is some relief. You say: We have good fire protection, good police protection, good light, good water, good ffavements on our streets, but the result of the federal tax you do not see. Interest on your debt must be paid. We have to collect the tax and people do not feel quite so willing to pay it as they do when they are called upon to pay other taxes. However, we are bound to make these collections, and those who are charged with this duty should be housed in proper quarters; and the public who pay the taxes should also have decent buildings in which to transact business. As an hon. member has said, it takes a good part of a day to hunt up the different offices; and while those who are constantly dealing with the Customs department such as brokers, who are conversant with the topography of the place, are able to find their way about, this is not the case with strangers. The first time I went to Toronto on business with the department I was at a loss to locate the dif-

Supply-Customs
ferent branches, so that I know what inconvenience the general public have to put up with. I am in complete sympathy with hon. gentlemen in this matter, and if the Minister of Public Works will back me up I am even willing to recommend that something be brought down in the supplementary estimates to meet the situation.
Cannot the Minister of Finance help you?
I would rather tackle the Minister of Public Works; he is easier. Perhaps the two of us might get after the Minister of Finance. I agree that the present quarters are inadequate.

In Toronto not
only is there a lack of proper accommodation for the Customs department, but there is in that city lying idle a railway station which cost a great deal of money. That building has been out of use now for three or four years and may continue unoccupied for as long a period again. If the minister would urge his colleague the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) to do something towards straightening out matters in Toronto the two railways could be asked1 to get together and find a solution for the situation. If proper steps were taken the entire public of Toronto could be better accommodated not only in connection with the buildings of the Customs department but also in regard to railway accommodation. The railway situation in Toronto is one of the biggest questions at the present time, and the whole matter has been held up indefinitely owing to some misunderstanding between the Dominion government and the city. I see no reason why it should not be settled, and I appeal to the government now to take some steps in the matter.
Is the hon. member suggesting that we should use the station as it stands now for a long room, and the basement as an examining warehouse?

What I am urging the government to do is to settle the railway problem in Toronto which has been in abeyance for ten years. That station has been idle for a considerable time now, and I am advising the government to take up all these questions together, with a view to providing proper accommodation for the people of Toronto not only in regard to the buildings that are necessary for the Customs department but also in connection with the station. I wish the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) were here himself; I would press upon
him as the head of the government the importance of getting settled this condition of congestion in connection with the National Railways, the Canadian Pacific Railway and these various offices.

I do not want to repeat anything that has been already said but I hope that the minister realizes the great inconvenience to which the people are put in Toronto by the lack of proper accomodation in the Customs department. We appreciate the kind words the minister has to say for Toronto, but we have been hearing this sort of thing now for some three years. Let me ask the minister pointedly, has he made any demand on the Public Works department for adequate accommodation? Let him get down to cold facts.

I have repeatedly made such a demand; every trip I have made to Toronto has served to impress me with the necessity for proper accommodation there, and I have never come back without emphasizing that necessity.

All I can say is, then, that .the minister ought to have more influence with his colleague who is in charge of the Public Works department. It is the duty of the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) to see that the city of Toronto is supplied with the necessary buildings to accommodate the public, and we look to him to have this done.
Could the Minister of Public Works be induced to say a word or two on this occasion?

I shall be glad
to do so. It is well known that Toronto requires new buildings; in fact, this has been known for some time, even before this government came into power. But it is also well known that there has been practically no construction of public buildings in Canada since the early part of the war, so that there is a great shortage of accommodation in the various services throughout the whole countin'. Up to the present time the government has not seen fit, nor indeed has it been possible, to undertake any large construction programme. I am not sure that it is the wish of parliament that such a programme should be undertaken. I remember very well the debate that took place a few weeks ago in regard to the construction of this building; at that time there was evident an opinion that this national edifice should not be completed, but that further construction should be delayed for five years. I have been in
Supply-Customs

Toronto, in Montreal and in other centres in Canada, and I know that there is need of construction work to be done; at Winnipeg, I may remark, I was impressed with that necessity. We fully appreciate the desirability and the necessity for improved facilities in these places in order that the various departments may carry on comfortably. But the matter is more than a mere question as between the Minister of Public Works and any other individual minister; it is a matter that affects the whole people of Canada, a matter of taxation.
Do I understand the Minister of Public Works to say that no public buildings are being put up at the present time?

I did not say
that.

Is there not a post office
being built at Sackville, New Brunswick?

A very small
building.
And another one at Kamloops?
I believe so.

I am sorry
that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King, Kootenay) seeks to compare the expenditure of further moneys on this building, which I should have thought was good enough for any of us to do business in as we have it now, with the expenditure of money in connection with what is undoubtedly an absolute necessity. There is no parallel whatever between the two cases, and my hon. friend is hard put to it when he tries to draw such a comparison. There can be no parallel between building an ornamental tower and constructing a commercial building which will facilitate the business of the country; there is no comparison between expenditures for ornamental lighting in this building and expenditures on public works which are long ' overdue. I will ask the Minister of Public Works to be kind enough to tell us what amounts are now paid in Toronto for accommodation which the minister himself admits is absolutely necessary, the present condition according to him being entirely unsatisfactory.

I shall be glad
to give that information when that particular matter in the estimates of my department is under discussion. Of course, I have not the information before me now.

It is a large
sum of money in any case, as I think the minister will admit; and if it were capitalized it would secure a building the revenue from which would look after the debt. In other words the country would really be at no extra expense whatever.

It could be
made an investment.

Yes, I hope
the Minister of Public Works will give us that information later on. In the meantime we note that the Minister of Customs has made his demand for this accommodation. I should like to ascertain from him what sort of building he demanded and where, in his opinion, it ought to be erected. He might also tell us the size together with other details so that we may know just what the business of the city actually requires in this regard.

My hon. friend has asked
me if we have taken any steps towards the erection of a new building, and what kind of building we have in mind. When I came into office I was presented with a plan which,
I was advised, had been prepared before the old building was torn down. It was a plan of a business building, a building with no frills on it, but designed for business purposes and to afford comfort both to the public and the employees. It was to be erected on the old location on Front street between Yonge and Bay. The site had' been already purchased, had it not?
Yes.

I would not have any
objection to the plan. It may be ahead of the present requirements, but Toronto is growing and the building would not be too big a few years hence.
The department, I understand, are already in possession of prepared plans, which they are satisfied with? And they have the land?

What is the

Speaking offhand,
I ivould say yes. I will bring down definite information in a few days.

If we are paying rentals equal to the carrying charges of a new building, and suffering all the inconveniences consequent upon the business of the department being transacted in several offices on different streets of the city, surely it is a wise thing for the government to provide 4 p.m. proper accommodation, and surely every member of the government will support the Minister of Customs to this end. I have not got the date.

I do not say there is a mistake. There is a regulation construed in a certain way that establishes a certain rule and then it is altered for particular people. The people in the business say this contradiction makes the regulation unworkable. The manufacturer does not object to the regulation so long as it is construed in the one way, but they point out the impossibility of complying with a regulation which has two constructions.

It is certainly not a fair statement to say that we are altering the regulation for certain people. I do not think the Department of Customs merits such an accusation, or any of the officers either. Does this refer to the sales tax or to customs duty?

It refers to the regulation dealing with whiffletrees and doubletrees. First of all it is held that these are a part of a wagon and then the regulation is made, as I understand it, that they are not to be so considered. The trade is first of all notified that these are not to be considered part of a wagon then a change is made and the importer is allowed to bring them in as wagon parts. That is the point I am making.

That would not be a regulation; that must be an interpretation by the collector or one of the appraisers or officers at the port who receives these articles. That would not be a subject for regulation. In the first place legislation is passed and when it has gone into effect an appraiser or an officer at one port may give it an interpretation entirely different from that of an officer or appraiser at another port. My hon. friend believes that in this case the proper interpretation has not been given. Very well, I will look into the matter. I cannot say offhand at what port this interpretation was given. Can my hon. friend say what port it was?
I think his officers will tell the minister that what I say is absolutely correct-that first of all a regulation was made-	j....,

The wrong word often

I wish to protest against
the increase in this vote. Here is an item that is increasing in amount year by year. Notwithstanding the fact that the government has gone at least a small step in the direction of free trade the vote for our pre-

ventive service this year is materially increased. It seems that we keep a little army of inspectors in foreign countries who demand to see the books of manufacturers there, and adopt other vexatious measures, under the impression that they are falsifying their invoices. I know of one exporter who came all the way to Canada from Europe to find out why his invoices would not be accepted by the Canadian customs authorities as they are in other countries to which he sends his goods. I think we are carrying this kind of thing to an uncalled for and unreasonable extent, and many of these inspectors employed on this work in foreign countries might just as well be recalled. Owing to these unreasonable and vexatious restrictions we are becoming a byword among the trading nations of the world. When our manufacturers complain that they cannot get rid of their goods it is possibly due to the atmosphere of suspicion which our actions have created in outside countries.
Do I understand my hon. friend's remarks to apply to the preventive service as a whole, or to the investigators of values that have been stationed in various countries.
Particularly the investigators of values.

I think these officers are
a necessity. It is all very well for my hon. friend to say that we ought to take the prices at the figures mentioned in the invoice, but let me say that we very seldom find cases where the figures on the invoice presented to the purchaser are not from 35 to 50 per cent higher than the figures in the invoice presented to the customs authorities. I do not think that is fair because the revenue of the country suffers. Putting to one side the question of the interests of the manufacturers I do not consider that to be a very proper proceeding.

Will the minister say that
is really the case?

It has been the case and
it still is. That is the reason we have to adopt protective measures in the interest of the revenue. In the United States the face value of the goods is not accepted. Over there they go to greater length than we do. We investigate and we say "if you are not dumping here well and good." But the United States reserve to itself the right to put an appraisement on the goods. They not only ascertain the cost but they fix 178$
their own appraisement. It they choose to price the goods at 100 per cent more, they do it and it stands. I think the investigation of values that we are making is a measure of protection, not in the sense of protection to the manufacturer but a protection to the revenue. Suppose there is an invoice relating to an importation of silk or other material from the United States or Japan and the quantity is given as 500 yards worth fifty cents a yard; when you go to the purchaser you find there are 1,500 yards worth $1.75. The revenue is being cheated out of so much, and that is the reason that we have a suspicion as to the good1 faith of those who are shipping, or as to the truthfulness of the figures on the invoice or manifest. We have investigators of value to make reports and the people who have imported are penalized according to the Customs Act.

I will tell my hon. friend. In the first place he must realize that there are not only ports where you obtain revenue, but there are ports where you do not get any revenue, but by means of which you send revenue to the other ports. That is the preventive service. You never know what you gain by the preventive service, because you are preventing smuggling. An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. If these ports were open smuggling would go on galore. Even with that $25,000 of expenditure, I am satisfied that we are bringing in, in proportion to the amount spent, just as much money as is brought in by the port of Toronto or the port of Montreal. That is to prevent smuggling and bootlegging and to see that people who are bringing goods in from the outside pay the duty on them. It has never been criticised and it is a necessity in this country. We have a large country; we have an extensive coast line on both the Atlantic and the Pacific, and everybody knows that a great deal of bootlegging or liquor smuggling and other smuggling is going on, not only by sea, but by land. Ministers of the gospel, men in high civic rank, mayors of municipalities, are weekly, if not' daily, after me to put more men in those ports in order to prevent bootlegging and smuggling. My hon. friend need not be scandalized. If we do away with those men and stop that expenditure of $25,000 or $30,000, which he says we are spending for nothing, millions of dollars will not come into the treasury because goods will be smuggled in without paying any duty at all. They are used as clearing houses for statistical purposes and for knowing exactly what ships contain. A preventive service is necessary in a country like this where we have a long coast line and where we are having a great deal of trouble inland also. In the newspapers every day there are accounts of cigarette smuggling, liquor smuggling. It may surprise my hon. friends if I tell them that spirits are coming into Canada from the United States*; silk and other things are also coming in. If we did not have the preventive

but if the officer had been within his duty, the duty charged would have been a specific duty of, I think, three cents a pound on the net weight of the raisins, and then an ad valorem duty of 35 per cent on the value of the carton. I do not think duty was paid on the weight of the container.

I think I shall be able to
convince the minister at another time if I have an opportunity, because I have the cus-
Supply-Customs

toms superintendent's ruling. I think I am right in saying that the merchant pays duty on the value of the box and what is contained in the box.

I do not want my hon.
friend to believe that I am contradicting him. He may have done that. If he has done it, it was done wrongly, because he ought not to have paid duty on the weight of the container. He ought to have paid duty on the net weight of tne raisins and then an ad valorem duty on the container. If my hon. friend will bring the case before me, I shall be glad to look into it.

On April 16, I asked for a copy of all letters and other documents between the federal government and the government of Saskatchewan on the question of licenses for export liquor houses. It	took	just	fifty days	for	this	reportto be laid on the Table. It was placed on	the Table yesterday	and I	was inmy	office	reading this report,	and	I hadgot about half through it, when I was notified that this discussion w'as on. This is not giving	us a	fair	opportunity	to	present our
case. As the government surffiy knows, about June 21 or 23 there is to be a referendum in Saskatchewan in connection with the liquor business, and there has been a controversy between this government and the Saskatchewan government as to who is responsible for the control of those export liquor houses. The reason I asked that this correspondence be placed on the Table was so that we could fix the responsibility. I think this discussion should not be closed to-day in justice to all parties concerned.

How would that interfere
with the election?
I want to have an opportunity to look through this return. The liquor interests of both governments are passing the buck when we nail them either in this House or in Saskatchewan.

I do not pass the buck.
I hang on to the buck.

I am going to hang
on just now for a minute. I interviewed the minister in his office and told him that we could not get them nailed down either provincially or here. He told me then that he did not pass the buck; but both parties deny the whole responsibility.

What responsibility? My
hon. friend is talking about export bonded warehouses.

Yes. The minister
stated two sessions ago that he did not issue a license except on the signed request of the Attorney General of Saskatchewan. During a by-election in my constituency last fall the Attorney General of Saskatchewan denied any responsibility in the matter.

Were there any licenses
issued?

Yes there have been
bonded warehouses there. What I want is the assurance of the minister that we shall have another opportunity to bring this matter up this session.

Were there any licenses
issued for what are commonly called import for export warehouses? Such houses do not exist as a matter of fact, but for the purposes of the discussion we will accept that term. Were any licenses issued for those houses since I became Minister of Customs?
They are doing business, I know that.
Have there been any licenses issued for these bonded warehouses since I have been Minister of Customs from January 1, 1922?
They have been continuing in business. '
The hon. gentleman is not explicit, and I will assume no responsibility for anything but what I myself have done.
I asked for the correspondence to be laid on the table, and I will make this charge now, that that correspondence has not all been brought down.
Let us know what is missing.

I will not. I have already said that it has not all been laid on the Table. I saw a letter written by the Saskatchewan government to the federal government and I can tell the minister that the file does not contain that particular communication. How does he expect me to answer his question when I have not been supplied with the information I have asked for?

It might be in my private file; I do not know. My hon. friend says that I am passing the buck. Well, I am entitled to know, I want to know, and I ought to know, what licenses I have issued in the province of Saskatchewan for these bonded warehouses of the kind the hon. gentleman speaks of, since I have been Minister of Customs.

Supply-Customs
If the file had been laid on the table as promptly as it should have been, and if all the information had been submitted, I should be able to answer the minister.
The file will not tell you; you ought to know.
I have not seen all the correspondence.
I do not object to my hon. friend making a field day of this if he wants to.

Are these not annual
licenses?
The excise are; the customs are not.
Are not these particular ones referred to, annual licenses?
Yes.
Then the minister must have issued some.
There are no excise licenses in Saskatchewan and those are the only annual licenses that are issued.

Are there no export
licenses?
There is no such thing as an export license.

How is it that these
houses exist?
There are bonded warehouses but no export houses.

Quite evidently there are some houses in existence and the confusion seems to be in regard to the name. The minister might tell us what is the proper designation of these houses and once we get that we shall know what we are talking about and shall be able to find out whether any licenses have been issued or whether they are renewals from year to year which I presume is what the hon. member wants to know or just what the situation really is.

Warehouses are licensed by the provinces for the storage of duty-paid liquor and once the duty is paid we have nothing more to do with the liquor. If anyone buys a coat and he pays the duty on it the government has no more responsibility in connection with the transaction; and similarly the moment the duty is paid on this liquor we are through with it. The importers might then want to put the liquor in a warehouse
to keep it until it could be exported and the province grants a license for this purpose. But this department has nothing to do with that.
Never had.
Never had; the duty is paid on the liquor and thereupon the department's responsibility ceases.
Is it an import duty?
An excise duty or an'import duty-
It would not be an import duty if the liquor was to go out again.

Why not? I might import liquor with the view of exporting it again. Before any liquor can be taken out of the control of the Dominion government whatever is due upon it must be paid, and when that money is paid the owner of the liquor can do what he likes with it so far as the department is concerned. In order that the liquor might be kept in the province however the provincial government consented to the establishment of bonded warehouses and they charged so much a case, or whatever it might be; at any rate they levied a tax for allowing the liquor to remain in the province so that the owner might get rid of it at his convenience. But the matter was one within the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities, and with it we had nothing whatever to do after, as I say, the duty had been paid us.

The minister's present
statement seems to conflict considerably with the statement of the Attorney General of Saskatchewan which I read a short time ago. Speaking in the House on April 6, 1922, in reply to a question asked by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), the minister made a statement which was not nearly so direct as his remarks to-day. And that is what I complain of. If the minister is not entirely satisfied that what he said then was correct he should at least make it plain to the House.

My hon. friend must be
careful to make the proper distinction. What we issue is a license for warehouses for the storage of liquor on which duty has not been paid. That liquor, so to speak, is under the King's guard. But when the duty is paid we are no longer concerned with the liquor, and if the provincial law forbids the keeping of liquor in the province it is none of our

Supply-Customs

business. When the duty is paid to us the provincial government can seize the liquor so far as we are concerned; but so long as the liquor is in the keeping of the Department of Customs, in the bonded warehouses kept for the storage of liquor on which no duty has been paid, it cannot be touched, the theory being that the King has control of it. But evidently the province considered that it would be unfair to the owners of liquor to seize it without an opportunity being given these people to dispose of it, and they themselves established bonded warehouses or storage warehouses, or what is called export houses,-you may call them what you like-to take care of the liquor in the meantime. The owners could not dispose of the liquor within the province but had to export it. But that was exclusively a provincial affair, without the jurisdiction of the Department of Customs; it was, I emphasize, exclusively within the control and jurisdiction of the province.
What licenses have been issued or renewed in Saskatchewan during the last twelve months?

Not one in the province
of Saskatchewan.

What I want to know
from the minister is; not the description of these houses, in which I am not so much interested, but whether or not the houses were established with or without the consent of the attorney general of the province. The Attorney General of Saskatchewan says:
The attorney general of this province-and remember I am the attorney general-never gave any consent to the establishment of any bonded warehouses or liquor export houses.
That is the point we want to get at; we want to know whether the provincial authorities had to consent to the establishment of these houses or not.

I think I have explained
the matter fairly fully. I have pointed out that when the duty is paid my control ceases. I could not grant any licenses of this kind inasmuch as I have no authority whatever to do so. I pointed out that these storehouses or warehouses were established evidently for the purpose of allowing those persons who owned liquor at the time the Temperance Act came into effect to dispose of that liquor in such a way that they would lose nothing. But that was done entirely and exclusively by the provinces. Whether the matter was under the direction of the attorney general or of the superintendent,

or whether it was managed as it is in Ontario, I do not know. At all events neither the Department of Customs nor any officer thereof had anything to do with the matter.

Were there no licenses issued in connection with these houses? Let me again read the question which the right hon. the leader of the opposition put in April 1922:
Mr. Meighen: Is it not a fact that the licenses were granted under the approval of the attorney general of the province?
Mr. Bureau: That has been and still is the policy of the department. We do not grant any licenses unless we get the approval of the attorney general attached to the petition for the license; at the same time we have the designation of the warehouse by him.
This is at variance with what the minister now tells us.

That relates to the storage of liquor in bond when the duty has not been paid. When the duty has not been paid and you want to store the liquor the license comes from the department; but when the duty is paid we have absolutely no control over the matter. My hon. friend is now referring to liquor in bond upon which no duty was paid. When the Temperance Act came into force, just before importation was prohibited, if any one wanted a bonded warehouse established to store liquor he made application for it. I said that the policy of the department had been, and was then, not to issue a license except with the consent of the man in charge of the operation of the temperance or liquor act or whatever else it might be in the province.

Now we are getting a little nearer the question. Am I to understand that the minister stands strictly by this statement that no licenses were issued in Saskatchewan without the consent of the attorney general?
Licenses for bonded warehouses where liquor was in bond duty unpaid; not export warehouses. I want the distinction to be dearly understood.
The attorney general mentions specifically bonded warehouses or liquor export warehouses.
That is his business, not mine.

What would the attorney general have to do with the establishment of a bonded warehouse, which is established only

Supply-Customs
for the purpose of collecting duty? Why would the minister ask the attorney general's consent foi that? I understood the matter as it has been read from Hansard; I thought it was export warehouses.

No. When anybody wanted to import liquor, before the importation of liquor was prohibited, he had to get a bonded warehouse, unless he paid duty. To get this bonded warehouse he had to obtain the consent of the Department of Customs and Excise. The department got all the necessary information, but before issuing the license they always wrote to the man in authority-the attorney general, I think, in Saskatchewan- and got his consent. That was not a regulation; that was the policy established in December 1916. When I came in the officials asked me if they should continue it, and I said, "Yes, it is only proper that where they have temperance or prohibition legislation they should be advised of the fact that such applications are being made in order to give them a chance to present their objections, if they have any to the licenses being granted." We continued that policy until lately. But that is not an export warehouse. The export warehouse is for duty-paid liquor, and when the duty is paid it is under the authority of the province.
Suppose the province had not agreed at all, what would be the consequence?
After the duty was paid?

No, no. I am referring to the policy established in 1916. I know there was a policy requiring the initiation of the provincial authorities. I cannot remember going into it in detail, but my general impression is that it related to export warehouses. I may be wrong in that.
You are mistaken surely.

Supposing it was as the minister says, just a bonded warehouse for the purpose of importation and to enable the owner to hold liquor until he paid his duty, and the province did not consent; then there would be no power of importation at all?
If the province did not give its consent or made any objection to the issue of the license, we would not grant it.

The minister says that
that policy was continued from 1916 until last December. What policy was established in its place?

None.

Well, are there any
bonded warehouses now?
There are.

As long as the bonded
warehouses continue, is not the policy continuing?

They were in force at the time; we did not issue any new licenses for bonded warehouses, except for distilleries. I am informed that there are now ten less than there were when I took charge of the Customs department.

I presume the province did not ask for their continuance:	Is that
the reason?

The importers themselves did not ask for their continuance. Application is not made by the province, but by the individual who is the owner of the bonded warehouse. If he did not ask for a renewal of the license, it lapsed.

The improvement in
policy is really the making a virtue of necessity.
I do not know-it is the virtue of a good example.

When the minister
made the statement which the member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) has just read, did he receive any protests from the Saskatchewan government?
Protests against what?

Did the Saskatchewan
government protest to your department against the correctness of the statement which the member for Mackenzie has just read?
I would have to look up the files. I do not remember; maybe.
The statement was made out there during the by-election that they did protest very vigorously.

I was not at the by-election; whatever statements were made then I am not going to be held responsible for. I am satisfied that hon. gentlemen
6 p.m. will make statements at by-elections which they would not make on the floor of the House.

The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) will agree with thatl
Supply-Customs
I saw a copy of a letter of protest in the hands of the attorney general, so I considered that pretty good evidence that a protest was made.
It is a pretty good presumption. The letter may have gone astray in the mails.
There is no copy of the letter on the file; that is why I am not satisfied.
I do not think that insinuation is fair. I have had letters go astray in the various departments.
Oh, oh.

To those who are used to the pure, all is pure, Mr. Chairman. Those who smile must have been the abstractors of letters. But I would not have any objection to producing any protest. If a protest was made about issuing a license, and no license was issued, where is the harm in the statement I made? I do not see any. If no license was issued, I had no consent to ask.
But here is the point: You made the statement that you did not authorize the issuing of any license without the written request of the Attorney General of Saskatchewan.
No, no.
The minister says no, that is not right; and further, before that a protest was made as to the responsibility for it.
I want my friend to stick to this: I have nothing whatever to do with export warehouses; it is the bonded warehouses that I am concerned with.
Mr. Chairman I do not wish to take any more time of the committee, but I should like an assurance that we shall have a chance to discuss this matter later.

I would ask that this item be allowed to stand for a little while.

Curing the recess I had inquiry made to find out if any licenses had been granted to private parties for bonded warehouses in Saskatchewan-the officers went down to the department to investigate it-and I find that none were granted. The only licenses that have been granted since I took charge of the department are the licenses to the official vendors, no others. So the point in dispute seems to have disappeared.
Does the minister mean the official vendors in Saskatchewan?
Yes.
I should like the item to stand for a little while so that an opportunity would be afforded of looking through the papers. In the meantime the minister could take up another item.
I have no objection.
The licenses that were issued were yearly licenses to private parties?
They were issued to bonded customs warehouses.
Yes, but they are yearly licenses.
No they are not yearly.
Does the minister mean that a permanent license is given a man, that it is not a yearly license?
If he has got a bonded warehouse for storing intoxicating liquors he must have a permit.
Yes, but for how long?

Until the license is revoked, or until he abandons it.

Supply-Customs
Subject to revocation at any time?
Yes.
I should like to make my position clear with regard to the question raised before recess. In the first place I am opposed to prohibition or coercion in any sense.
Hear, hear.

I want that distinctly understood. The point I raised however was that I felt the department were losing some revenue over these seaworthy vessels carrying this liquor supposed to be for export. We might assume that each vessel would carry a thousand cases. At a duty of $15 a case this would represent $15,000. It would only need one hundred of such trips to make a loss of revenue to the country of $1,500,000. I merely make this statement for the purpose of explaining my position.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the intention, Mr. Minister, to allow this item to stand?

If there is any further
information my hon. friend desires I am willing to give it. The bone of contention seems to be that I should not have issued licenses without the permission of the provincial authorities. I find from the records of the department there have been no licenses issued to private individuals for bonded warehouses; so that I could not have granted licenses without their permit, none having been issued.

Here is the position;
the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) is not clear on this whole matter; it is a big and important question, and this return should have been brought down sooner. It was asked for fifty days before it was laid on the table and we have not had time to read it. If the committee will go on with another item, we will be ready in an hour's time.

Then is it understood
that this item stands for to-night? I should like to look over the correspondence. Has the minister found the missing letter?

I have not had time to
look for it. I do not know 'what it is.

I thought that would
be more important than the point the minister did look up.

If I understand rightly,
the missing letter was a protest against the issuing of licenses by the federal authorities.

No, it was against
this government stating that it was for the Saskatchewan government to take all responsibility for the issuing of the licenses. They disclaim all responsibility. The minister made the statement that he did not issue a license without the signed request of the Attorney General of Saskatchewan.

No, there is a misunderstanding. I said without the consent-not at the request. I do not want it to be understood that I wanted it to come from the provincial government. If I said that, I did not state what I had in my mind. The answer I made was that before issuing licenses we always got the consent of the local authorities in charge of the administration of the liquor laws in the province.

Could the minister tell
us how many export liquor licenses have been issued throughout the Dominion?

My hon. friend was not
here when I explained that. When the duty is paid on liquor, if the provincial law prohibits the possession of liquor within the limits of the province, we have nothing to do with it. If the owner of the liquor wants to keep it for the purpose of export, so as not to lose the whole thing, he obtains authority from the provincial government. That is what they call the provincial export license. The government charges him so much and allows him to keep the liquor in the province, and he exports it later on; but we have nothing to do with that.

We were talking this afternoon about the inspector who places the value on apples. Would the minister inform the committee whether the officer came all the way from British Columbia to Winnipeg to value apples that had been imported from the state of Washington by a Winnipeg jobber; and if so, what value he placed on apples imported from Washington last winter?

Mr. Mowat, who has this
particular duty to perform, is in Vancouver and goes to Winnipeg to examine invoices and prices and to investigate conditions.

What value did he place
on apples coming from Washington last winter?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I question if items
of the tariff can be brought up under this item. Matters of administration can be discussed.
Supply-Customs

I do not object to the
question, but I could not say offhand. My hon. friend will understand that we do not get reports of all these things, and if we did I could not carry them in my mind, and would not have any record of them here.

I do not want to ask any
question that is not in order, but it seems to me this is the only place that we can ask any questions regarding the administration of the Dumping Act and I feel that this is the proper place to ask the question. Would the minister be willing to lay on the Table of the House the reports he got from these officers showing the value they placed on these apples?

These appraisals and valuations are made by the officers. They must appear on the invoice in the particular port. If the invoice contains a certain price for the apples, and that price is changed by the appraiser, it must appear on the invoice.

Is the minister aware of the fact that sometimes this dumping duty has been levied by his officers on shipments of apples after part of the apples have been sold by the importer to the retailer? Could the minister not find some way of administering the act that would not inflict this hardship on the importer?

In speaking of these
apples, all importers are told when they bring in commodities or products that their entries are subject to correction, and subject to the appraisal which has to be made. They are all warned of that.

Could the minister not have these valuations made so that the importers could be told when the apples are cleared through the customs that the duty would be so much, and not have the duty imposed after the man has cleared his apples and possibly sold most of them to retailers?

We must get the shipment before we can make an investigation. We do not know what the duties are going to be. After the shipment is in we make the investigation, and then these people know exactly where they stand, because the appraiser makes his report and assesses the value. But- the shipment must be made first.

I may be misinformed, but
I have had letters from some of the importers stating that they have' [been assessed for dumping duties after they have had the apples in their warehouse for some time and

after they have actually sold most of them to the retailers. I understood the minister to say this afternoon that the United States were dumping a lot of poor apples into Canada.

I do not want to be understood as saying that. I just reported a conversation I had with an American at Vancouver. I did not say that I believed it or that I did not believe it, or that it was true or false. I reported it for what it was worth. I did not make it my statement.

The minister certainly left
the impression on my mind that he or his agent had acted on this information when they levied the dumping duty. Is the minister aware that these same British Columbia fruit men are shipping hundreds of cars of apples to the United States every year? I would like to know whether his appraisers have examined the books of the British Columbia growers and found out what they were charging for these apples they were shipping to the United States, Great Britain, Mexico, Sweden, Germany and Japan. If not he does not know whether he is making the people on the prairies pay more for their apples than people in those foreign countries.

It is not for us to look
into shipments made by our people. If they ship to Mexico, the Mexican authorities are there to protect themselves. If they ship to the United States, the United States authorities are there to protect themselves. The United States authorities do not examine the invoice of their shippers when they ship to Canada. It is up to the Canadian authorities to look into them and to protect themselves.

Will the minister be good
enough to inform the committee who is looking after the people on the prairies that would like to get apples?

I suppose each individual
who desires apples ought to be able to look after himself and get them. I do not presume they want any particular tutor or guardian for that purpose. I know when I want an orange or an apple, I do not go to my neighbour, I go out and get it.

They do not want some
appraiser going around and penalizing these fruit jobbers when they import a car of apples. The minister has shown that these people on the prairies had better get somebody to look after their interests.

That is their business.

Supply-Customs

I wonder if I would be in
order if I asked the minister on what basis his officers are now setting the value of goods imported from Germany? What procedure are they following in fixing the value of those goods for duty purposes?

That is determined by the law which reads:
In the case of importation of goods, the manufacture or produce of a foreign country, the currency of which is substantially depreciated-
That would include Germany.
-the value for duty shall not be less than the value that would be placed on similar goods manufactured or produced in the United Kingdom and imported from that country if such similar goods are made or produced there. If similar goods are not made or produced in the United Kingdom, the value for duty shall not be less than the value of similar goods made or produced in any European country the currency of which is: not substantially depreciated.
That is a question of law, not of regulation.

Some of us are getting the
impression that the Customs department is a law unto itself, and that is the reason I asked the minister the question. Could he tell this committee whether it is a fact that Germany is now quoting her goods, not in German currency, but in either American or British currency?

Whether they quote them
in German marks or American dollars or Canadian dollars does not alter the value of the currency in Germany. If they quote $10 for a thing that is worth $20 in England, naturally it will be appraised as being worth $20, the value of the goods in England according to the law that I have just cited. Whatever currency they quote does not make any difference as to the value of the currency in the country of origin.

I think it is well that the
committee should get all the information they can in regard to this question, because I will admit that I have not all the information I would like. I have lately received from a gentleman who is in the importing business in Montreal some information regarding this matter. I do not want to take up much time, but I will read a memorandum that he gave me in regard to scissors. This is just one of the items, but it will serve as an example:
The scissors and shears are supplied to Canada to a great extent by United States manufacturers. We understand that Great Britain is not equipped in the industry to supply her own demands, but that she imports annually large quantities of United States and German manufactured shears and scissors for her own use as well as for her export trade.
It seems absurd to use the cost of British made scissors and shears as a base in Canada for the cost of German scissors and shears for duty purposes. The
result is generally a workman, working girl, or farmer has to pay for the extra valuation for duty purposes. Under present rulings, it raises the cost of these scissors and shears to nearly double the price of what they should be, as the duty on these goods-
I think he means to include the sales tax.
-amounts to 113.4 per cent of the cost. The application of the valuation taken from British goods does not give any more trade to Great Britain but gives a certain amount of additional trade to the United States of America, which thereby increases the unfavourable balance of trade against Canada.
This could be reduced by allowing the German-made scissors and shears to come into Canada at their real value.
I would be much obliged to the minister if he could inform us whether that is the way in which the duty is actually working out at the present time. That brings the duty and sales tax in some cases to over 100 per cent of the value of the goods.

I just explained to my
hon. friend that this was not a matter of regulation. Those scissors are imported from Germany. The currency is depreciated in Germany. They say the scissors are worth $10 or $5 a dozen. The value for duty purposes is the value of similar goods manufactured in England, as I have just said. That is a matter of law, not of regulation, and the customs collector has to follow the law. The law says that when goods are imported1 from Germany, Russia, Czechoslovakia, Austria, the value of the goods shall be the value of similar goods in England. That is the Customs Act as amended in 1922.

I am informed that this
country is maintaining trade agents in Germany. If we take into consideration the condition that Germany is in, how can we sell her any goods if we do not take goods from her? I am at a loss to know how we can continue to import goods if the duty and1 the sales tax against Germany amount to over 100 per cent. If the law is wrong, the minister is in the best position to know about that, and I think it is time he suggested some change in that law.

I have no control over
trade agents or trade conditions. I am administering the Customs Act. The question my hon. friend puts to me is: How is Germany to pay such a high duty? I explained to him that the duty on all goods coming from a country where the currency is depreciated is regulated by statute. I have no power to change it. Parliament is master of the situation; parliament can amend it, and if parliament chooses to say that goods
Supply-Customs

shall be valued at the currency of the mark, that is its business, not mine. My duty is to administer the act as I find it in the statute book. My hon. friend wants to be fair. He knows very well that I cannot change the provisions of the statute.

Is the minister trying to
give the impression that a private member could bring in any bill to amend the present act dealing with depreciated currency? He surely does not want to give that impression.

I do not give any impression at all. We all have the same rights in this House. When we think anything is wrong, it is our right to discuss it and to make suggestions. These amendments were made by the Minister of Finance. This is a question that comes under his jurisdiction. My hon. friend has not been deprived in any way of an opportunity of making suggestions or of expressing his views. I am stating to him my position. My hon. friend seems to be under the impression that by a regulation of the department we can remedy this. I am explaining to him that I cannot. If he wants an amendment to the Customs Act, let him suggest it. I do not say that he has the right to make any motion in regard to it, because it must come from the government. But so far no suggestion has been made in the matter; at least I have not heard any in the House. I am discussing the act as I find it and am trying to explain matters to the hon. gentleman as well as I can. If he thinks that this is a question that rests with the department he is under a false impression, because the department is bound to administer the act as it stands and the act provides that the measure of value of goods coming from Germany or from any other country whose currency is depreciated shall be according to a certain standard which is laid down; and I have no other means of valuing such goods. I do not say that the hon. member's views are either right or wrong; I am merely stating that it does not lie within my power to make any change.

I assure the minister I am not trying to be unfair to him. I wish he would say whether in his opinion the duty now collected on these goods coming from Germany is levied strictly in accordance with the regulations, or whether it is just possible that the inspectors are putting too high a value on the goods.

The officers are instructed to adhere to the law, and the law states clearly what shall be done; the goods shall be appraised at the value of similar goods made in England. I do not see that there is any other explanation I can give the hon. gentleman; the matter is perfectly clear in the act.

I will not bother the minister any further, but I would point out that although we have been discussing these estimates all afternoon we have secured very little information regarding the actual working of the Department of Customs. I am not criticising the minister at all in that respect, but I would urge him to suggest to his government that the estimates of some of the departments at least be submitted to some standing committee of the House and passed by that committee before being brought down to the House. This is what is proposed in regard to the estimates of the Minister of Railways, that they be submitted to a special committee of the House for consideration. This would greatly expedite the business of the House and I am sure hon. members would be able to discuss the estimates in a more intelligible manner. The result would be more satisfactory not only to the members themselves but also to the department and the country at large.

The committee has been
dodging around from one thing to another in such an erratic -way that I would not blame the minister for getting out of patience. But at the same time I must say that he has made one statement himself which is responsible for my getting up now; I refer to what the minister said about people being able to look after themselves when they wanted to buy fruit. Well, so far as that goes, I have reason to know that much as they would like to, they cannot possibly "look after themselves" at the present time under conditions as they are and with the dumping clause in operation against them. I know of one case where the fruit dealers in Edmonton desired to buy apples in Washington so that they might be able to supply the trade in their city at a cheaper rate than they were otherwise able to do. But from what I have learned there seems to be some question as to whether the dumping regulations were properly applied. The British Columbia apple dealers were unable to supply the particular apples required in this instance-winesaps

and when the Edmonton dealers tried to get them from the United States they discovered that the

Supply-Customs
dumping clause operated to their detriment. There was a question as to whether it was applied justly or not. I want to tell the minister that the people on the prairies would like to look after themselves, as he says, if they could; but it is impossible for them to do so with the dumping clause against them. If the British Columbia dealers were able to supply these particular apples the people would like to buy from them rather than go across the line. I think it is well worth the minister's while to take this matter into consideration; certainly the people of the prairies are at a disadvantage under present conditions. They were compelled in this instance to pay so much more for the apples when the dumping clause was brought into force that they were obliged to go without them.

What time of year was
it that the people in the prairies could not buy British Columbia winesaps?

They grow some of these apples in British Columbia but not very .many,' and the time I am referring to was during the fall season before I came here, the early part of the winter. I know that the British Columbia people did not have these particular apples at the time they were wanted, and when the dumping clause was brought into force it prevented the prairie people from getting them, the price being too high.

What the hon. gentleman has just said reveals to us the luxury in which the farmers of the western provinces live. Apparently there is only one kind of apple in the world which they will eat and it must be something very choice. Down in our province we will eat northern spies.
Or rhubarb.
Yes, and in large quantities.

You have no dumping
clause against you.
My hon. friend I think discovers that he has put his foot in it.

As to my foot, it is perfectly comfortable. My hon. friend comes from a place where the duty has nothing to do with the apples he buys; they cannot sell all the apples they raise in that community. Nevertheless they are telling us that the home market will make us all rich.

The problem of the hon. members who represent Toronto is not the same as the problems we have in the West,
and their ideas of luxury are no doubt different from ours. I have a list of telegrams which passed last fall between the fruit growers of British Columbia and the jobbers of Vancouver in which the latter contracted for a certain volume of fruit. I hesitate to put all these telegrams on Hansard and so I will summarize their contents; the telegrams are at the disposal of the minister at any time. The Vancouver jobbers contracted for the delivery of 25 cars of peaches, 15 cars of apricots and 5 cars of pears early in the season. Considerable advertising was done to convey to the people of Vancouver the importance and the duty of eating homegrown fruit. The season wore on, marketing conditions changed a little, and they found that they could sell fruit on the prairies at a better price and on a less discriminating market; so they forced the Vancouver people to get along with 5 cars of peaches, 3 cars of pears and considerably less than a car of apricots, so that they could sell extra fruit on the prairie market. The minister's department came to the rescue with the dumping clause. When the price got high in the prairies the suggestion was made to bring the fruit from the United States; some fruit was brought in but the minister's agent went to the prairies and put a valuation on that fruit which it never had and collected a duty which prohibited further importations. I would point out to the minister that he will have a very hard time convincing the people that that is what the dumping clause was intended for. He made the statement this afternoon that we might as well not have any statute at all in regard to the dumping clause as his department administers it. I cannot put any other interpretation on his words. I think it is very unfair to the people that his department should so administer the dumping clause as to create a condition of this kind.

Mr. Chairman, I think the words of my hon. friend (Mr. Kellner) prove beyond a shadow of doubt that the people of British Columbia were more than anxious to supply the needs of the prairie farmers when they cancelled the order which they had to ship apples to Vancouver. Now, in regard to the question of who is looking after the fruit needs of the prairie people, I understood that some time ago the Grain Growers' Association was handling the fruit for the prairie farmers, and as I have already stated in the House some of the prairie organizations were making 65 cents a box profit on British Columbia apples.
