Shame!

Yes, I should say so. I have that statement signed by the secretary of one of the Grain Growers' associations. With respect to the winesap apples which were being shipped in from the American side, Mr. Thomas Bulman, of the Okanagan, was here at the time and I took this question up with him. He told me that there were then in cold storage sixteen cars of the same kind of apples which he was anxious to get rid of.

Mr. Chairman, I have a word of explanation to offer in reply to the statement of the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. McBride) regarding the profit of the Grain Growers' Association on apples. He is quoting the price from a local association which, if I remember rightly, is the North Battleford association. The Grain Growers' Association buy apples wherever they can get them, whether from British Columbia or Washington. The local association at North Battleford was compelled by the rest of the distributing trade in that city to sell the apples at the price referred to, otherwise they were told they could not get their shelves replenished with any other line of goods. That is an instance of how the anti-dumping clause is applied on goods in western Canada and elsewhere to-day. The absurdity of applying a dumping duty to fruit coming into this country, particularly into western Canada, can easily be shown by the fact that at the time it was being so applied in western Canada to certain cars of apples from Washington the British Columbia apple growers or packers could not supply even the Vancouver trade and had to import the deficiency. The real reason for the dumping duty being applied on fruit in western Canada is because the British Columbia apple growers are exporting their best apples and want this added protection in order to get rid of their culls. Naturally we in the West object. Another absurdity of the application of the dumping clause is shown in the fact that when applying it to two cars of apples that came into Winnipeg last March Mr. Mowat was brought all the way from British Columbia a distance of 1,200 miles, to assess the duty. Could anything more absurd be imagined?
Does the hon. member contend that the dumping duty on fruit should be entirely eliminated? Is that his frank position?

I would say that it should
be. I say further that any apple growers in this country who cannot carry on with the advantage of a shorter freight haul and a 
30 cent per box duty ought to go out of business. Anyway, I serve notice on the British Columbia advocates of the dumping duty to-day that the plain people of the prairies are not going to tolerate its continuance much longer, and already relations are strained between the fruit distributors of the prairie provinces and the apple growers of British Columbia. To bring a man 1,200 miles to assess the dumping duty on two cars of apples in Winnipeg seems to me an utter absurdity. One would think that a duty of 30 cents a box would be quite sufficient advantage to any apple growers in any part of the Dominion. If it can be proven that the United States apple growers are sdling their apples for export at a lower price than for home consumption, then I say there is some justification for the dumping duty being applied; but in the case of apples which last year we could buy at Washington for 80 cents a box, the price at which they were being sold to any one in the United States, why was the dumping duty levied in western Canada? Because the British Columbia fruit growers claimed the United States growers should be getting $1.10 a box! I think the absurdity of the whole thing is plain to every member when I recall the fact that to-day we are maintaining an army of officers in all countries of the world to look after this business for our apple growers and manufacturers while we are collecting less than $130.000 in duty under the dumping clause.

Mr. Chairman, it is
apparent from the speech of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) and of certain other hon. members that they are very strongly disposed to eliminate all duties whatsoever. Now, the British Columbia fruit question has been explained time and again by members from that province, particularly by our friend, the late Mr. MacKelvie. The facts, as I understand them, are simply these: that at certain periods of the year the United States apple growers, owing to climatic and other conditions are able to produce their fruit a little earlier than their British Columbia competitors, and they not only supply their home market but also the market of Canada at the highest prices; later when the British Columbia apples are ripe our growers find the cream of the market has been taken by their competitors across the line, and in addition the home market is further depressed by the dumping of the surplus product from the States. The net result of eliminating the anti-dumping clause would accentuate the extremely hard times which the apple growers

of British Columbia are passing through; not only so, but many of the men who have invested thousands of dollars in their orchards and waited years for them to come into bearing in order to supply the home market would be put out of business.
Is the hon. member aware that there is a duty of 30 cents a box on apples?

Yes, but that protection is not sufficient at certain times of the year.
Mr. COOTE. Will the hon. member give to this committee any reason why the dumping duty applicable to natural products should not be the same as applied to. manufactured goods?

I do not see the relationship. I believe the dumping duty is applied to manufactured goods to protect home industries. Now so far as apples are concerned, and the fruit industry of British Columbia, it is onfy a periodical application of the dumping clause that is required; that is, it is put on when what we consider unfair means are being used. I would like to ask hon. gentlemen sitting to my left, as men not actuated by selfish motives, and I know they are not, whether they are disposed to use their power in this House in favour of a step which would save them only an infinitesimal amount on the cost of their fruit, but that would put out of business many thousands of men engaged in the ap,ple-grow-ing districts in the central portion of British Columbia, who have invested millions of dollars there, and in which the government has also made a huge investment? If it were a question, of trying to grow cotton around the north pole by artificial protection of an extreme kind, their arguments would be reasonable, but this is a question of protecting this industry only at certain given times of the year against unfair competition, and if we are going to maintain the unity which hon. gentlemen preach so strongly, consideration must be had for all parts of this country which are specially affected by foreign competition at particular times of the year. Let us have a little reciprocity in the concessions given from one end of this country to the other. What do we find so far as my friends to my left are concerned? They come down here with grqat political power-

Does the

I say that the anti-dumping clause should be applied to protect the business of fruit-growing in British Columbia against unfair competition at any time of the year.
I understood the hon. member to advocate only a perodical application of the anti-dumping clause.

No, I did not say that. I say that the necessity for its application is periodical; it is applied to meet a certain condition. This is an important matter for British Columbia, and I think before hon. gentlemen to my left decry the application of the anti-dumping clause they should be better informed on the investment that has been made in this industry and what it means to British Columbia, and when they look for tariff readjustments on machinery and. other articles they might have consideration for these fruit-growers in British Columbia who are tied up with their investments in this industry.

I want ,to take exception to
the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South that we should be better informed, and I would suggest to him that possibly he is not as well informed on the dumping act as applied to natural products as he might be; otherwise, he would have [DOT]answered the question I put to him a little while ago, when I asked him to give any reason why the dumping act which applies to natural products should not be the same as applied to manufactured goods. If he is well enough informed to lecture us in this regard, perhaps he can now answer that question.

I want to call the attention of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) to the fact that he is m

danger of putting the prairie farmer out of the business of eating fruit, and consequently of putting the British Columbia grower out of the business of raising apples.
Try Ontario apples.

Some Ontario apples we get are very good. We always find the top layer of the barrel good, but the rest are what they would not feed to their pigs. I do not wish to reflect on the fruit growers of Ontario. I do not know whether it was a high protectionist or a fruit grower that packed those apples. This question is a serious one, Mr. Chairman, for the prairies. We need fruit on the prairies, and British Columbia, on account of being nearer, should supply us with our fruit.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that this item concerns the expenditure of a department. There is no question here of whether a certain act is a proper act or not; it is simply a question of whether the expenditure is proper, and whether the law is being administered efficiently. This debate has continued for some time, and for nearly an hour hon. members have been wandering away from the subject matter.

I am sorry if I am out of order, Mr. Chairman. I hardly thought I was, because everybody has been saying about what he pleases on this item. When I remember what others have said, I can hardly think I am out of order. If you will allow me, Mr. Chairman, to encroach just a little further, I want to say that I know that the British Columbia land on which they are growing these apples is from three to four times the price it ought to be. We want apples in the prairie provinces, and we do not care whether we get Ontario or British Columbia apples, but we do want them at a price we can afford to pay. That is what we are interested in. We are not more selfish than other human beings, but we have been up against it hard enough in paying tariff duties on everything so that we have not much left now to pay for apples, and we want to eat apples. I think it is well worth while for this House to consider whether the dumping clause is not going to put us out of business of eating apples, and consequently put out of business the man who is growing apples. I do not think the dumping clause was applied last fall at the right time, and in the right place. In fact,
I do not know where the right place is; I have never been able to find that out; I think 
we should get rid of it altogether. I want the government, and the Minister of Customs particularly, to be mighty careful how he uses that anti-dumping clause, if it is possible for him to be careful.
Can the hon. member say what the application of the dumping duty adds to the cost of a box of apples?
I do not know exactly how much it amounts to on each box but it is enough in some cases to put us out of the business of eating apples.

Mr. Chairman, a question was asked a moment ago, a perfectly proper question I think, in regard to the administration of this dumping clause-why the clause which applies to manufactured articles is not equally applicable to natural products. The question I say is a fair one, and I think a very proper one. The reason is-the minister will correct me if I state it in any sense unfairly-that in the case of the manufactured article you have generally a fixed price which is easily ascertained in the country where the article is manufactured. In, perhaps, ninety per cent of the cases there are regular lists of prices Issued, and the article is of a nonperishable character. But with fruit you have an article that is not only perishable but variable-variable as to varieties, variable as to seasons, variable as to the quantity of the crop which always affects the price. So that from day to day there is no fixed price on fruit, it is something that is constantly changing. Secondly, while it is very simple to ascertain the market value of a manufactured article, it is exceedingly difficult to find the market value of fruit.
Will you explain why it is difficult to find?
Yes I am going to explain that. Take for instance the production of Strawberries, I use that, perhaps, as a more extreme type and more suited to making the explanation clear.
Make the explanation on apples.

I will make it with respect to strawberries first, and then I will take pears and apples. Now, strawberries are produced and they must be marketed at once; let two or three days elapse and the strawberries are unsaleable. The growers south of the line produce strawberries very quickly. If there happens to come a shower of rain it ripens the strawberry very quickly and turns

Supply-Customs
it into a soft condition not suitable for keeping any length of time. What they do south of the line, and it is a regular practice, is this:	They supply their home market-
Seattle, Spokane, and these other cities all through that area at cost price because the growers south of the line are well organized, and they have the home market under control. But the surplus they will dump into Vancouver, for instance, or into Calgary, or on a market they can reach at any price at all, because the amount they get is pure salvage, it is barely sufficient to meet expenses whatever the amount may be. It does not follow :hat they must make even the cost price of .he article because they have already protected their profit in the stabilized market south of the line.
In the home market?

In the home market.
Now then, in facing this situation the minister and his predecessor were called upon to find a dump that was applicable, and so we had a dump clause to this effect, that the Customs department would ascertain the cost of the production of the article and allow that price plus 10 per cent for profit, and that was the dutiable price to the Canadian market. Now we come to pears. I have in mind-and perhaps the minister's assistants could give the exact data in regard to this-an incident that occurred where nine carloads of pears were shipped on consignment into Calgary. They were shipped there simply at any price that could be secured for them-in fact they secured, if I recall rightly, a very low price, about one-third of the market value of these pears. Well, no Canadian grower could compete with a condition of that kind. Now take apples as to which my hon. friend (Mr. Coote) asked for an explanation. I will also reply to the question which was raised by my hon. friend from Glengarry (Mr. Kennedy) in which the suggestion is made that there was a period, perhaps, at the beginning of the season where the dump may be applicable. But you must remember this:	You
have apples coming on the market-I will give the British Columbia data as well as I can recall them-from the end of July, early harvest apples. Then you have the Graven-stein coming on in September; the Macintosh Red coming on about October; and then you have other varieties in November, the later varieties, the winter varieties which keep well. You have a long series of different varieties of apples some of which are only marketable during the particular two or three weeks that they come on the market.
Take early harvest apples. You cannot possibly, even with cold storage, keep them over perhaps a period of a month, or five or six weeks. On the other hand winter varieties can be kept over until spring. The dump therefore must be made applicable not simply at the opening of the apple season but its application must correspond to the coming on the market of the different varieties. Again we have exactly the same situation. We have in the Wenatchee country, in the Hood river valley, in Oregon and Washington, particularly in Washington, some very extensive orchards. The growers there pack all their apples very skilfully and the fruit is very carefully graded. The very high and fancy grades are saleable in every great city of the United States-New York, Chicago, St. Louis. Cincinnati, and Cleveland. Clear across the continent they have a splendid market for their number one grades at high figures.
Ten cents apiece.

Someone suggests that
they retail at ten cents apiece, at any rate they get very high figures for these fancy grades. But they have also second and third grades. For instance, their second grade is a good apple, a very excellent apple, and one which will market well, but it has not got the demand that the very fancy first grade has on the high priced market. Well, they seek to dump their surplus of seconds and thirds on the Canadian market-on the Canadian Northwest market if you like or any of the cities; indeed, they dump them into Vancouver just the same as they dump them into Calgary or Winnipeg. This competition is wholly and utterly unfair, as far as our fruit growers are concerned. I would say this to my hon. friends: I know this question has been discussed many times in years gone by, and the suggestion is made, "Why should not the prairie purchaser have the number one grade as well as anybody else?" There is no reason why he should not if he will pay the price. I want to say this, however, that for all ordinary purposes there are very few hon. members would discern very much difference between a good, general number two grade and a number one fancy grade. There is a little more uniformity of size, a little better colour perhaps, and more careful packing- it is a little fancier all round-but the number two grade is just as good. It is not a question of putting an inferior grade on the market at all; it is just simply a condition that develops in this industry.
Now, let me turn to the industry itself which calls for this dumping clause and the applies-
Supply-Customs

tion of it by the minister. My hon. friend said there was land in the Okanagan valley, where these apples are produced, that is three times above the value it should be. Well, I venture to say that in the case of the Okanagan growers this year-and I certainly regret that our late friend Mr. MacKelvie is not here because he had all this information at his finger tips-the great majority of them, fully 90 per cent of them came out at the end of the season with a complete loss on operation. Considering the price of land I venture to say further that the owners of these orchards in the Okanagan valley would be delighted if they could get a return covering the cost of production plus, say 2 per cent on the cost of this high priced land.

Does the hon. member for Vancouver Centre not think that if we had got rid of protection some time ago the fruit growers would have been in a better position because we on the prairies would have been able to buy their apples?

I am glad my hon. friend asks that question. I will tell him the history of the citrus fruit situation which illustrates where you would be if the protection had been taken off. If there had been no protection you would have had no development of the fruit industry in Biitish Columbia and very little in Ontario probably. About twenty years ago-and I recall the time very well because I dealt at that time very largely in the marketing of fruit and articles of that kind-we used to buy lemons and sell them retailed at twenty cents a dozen. That was the prevailing price for years, with perhaps an occasional rise in the middle of the summer season. Our oranges were sold according to grades and sizes up to thirty cents a dozen, and very rarely beyond that. At that time Canada bought its citrus fruit in California, Florida and the West Indies, but the California citrus fruit industry, organized under Mr. Shapiro and other organizers of that character secured first from congress a heavy prohibitive duty, which shut out the competition of the West India fruit in the American market; they secured absolute control of the American market, and then by the development of their industry they controlled the American market from the selling end, but not from the buying end. They supplied the citrus fruit to the American market just as they saw fit to send it, and: maintained the price. What was the effect of that on Canada? The effect upon Canada was that when the United States shut off the market from the West India fruit growers, these West India

concerns went out of business. We had been receiving West India fruit in Canada in competition with California fruit. When the West India fruit was shut off, we were confined to the California fruit; and for the last ten or fifteen years, I think I can say, the price of citrus fruit in Canada has been from two to two and a half times the price at which we could purchase it in the previous ten or fifteen years. And why? Because the citrus fruit growers in California fixed the price. We have no duty on lemons and oranges; they are absolutely free, and yet the price has doubled during that period. I obtained the prices in Seattle and Vancouver, Winnipeg and St. Paul, Buffalo and Toronto, and all corresponding places along the line, and in every case the citrus fruit was marketed in Canada at a slightly higher price than south of the line, although we have no duty on that fruit.

I was just wondering
what the prohibitive duty of the United States is.
I cannot give it offhand to my hon. friend, because I was not prepared for this discussion at all, but I would say perhaps thirty per cent.
Ad valorem?

Yes. I must give that answer subject to correction, because I am not certain. I made a very careful study of the citrus fruit situation, and I will give the House an illustration applicable to the administration of the dumping clause. The citrus fruit growers-I want this to be made perfectly clear-through the act and persuasion of congress, through prohibiting it, closed the market to the West Indian grower, and thus cut off that supply. Let me say this-and if the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low) were in his seat I would invite his attention to it-that when the West India delegates were in Ottawa, I think about 1920, and made an agreement with Canada under which we allbwed their products to come into Canada, they told us that they wanted to come in here with citrus fruit, and if we would give them a preference in our market for citrus fruit they would replant their lemon and orange groves, stimulate industry and go into the production of citrus fruit again. I am certain that if Canada had put a duty on citrus fruit, in a very few years we would be buying citrus fruit in Canada twenty-five to fifty per cent less than the price we pay to-day, and we would stimulate that trade. But that is on the side. If

Supply-Customs
the dumping clause is removed, or if the minister fails to administer this dumping clause in the interests of the Canadian producer, and if you add to that the removal of the meagre duty, I will venture to say, without the slightest hesitation-
Is that a thirty per cent duty?

Thirty cents a box, not thirty per cent-if these are removed the result will be, without any doubt, that the Canadian fruit grower will be squeezed and put out of business. I can take hon. members to the Okanagan to-day and show them orchard after orchard which has been abandoned during the last few years. An orchard goes to pieces in a couple of years beyond recall. What will be the result? Do you think you will get the fruit on the dumping basis? No, you will get it at prices dictated by the Washington and Oregon Fruit Growers' Association. There is no question about that. We have to face it. Let me say to my hon. friends who object to the application of this dumping clause that the growers of the Okanagan constitute perhaps one of the best co-operative agricultural or horticultural organizations in the country. They are splendidly organized. What for? Not to force Canadians to pay an unreasonable price. That is not it. They are organized to try and make a bare living out of their business and out of their chosen vocation. My hon. friend may say to me, "Well, they ought to have foreseen that", but you must remember that it takes from six to ten years to bring an apple tree into full bearing, and some take longer, while some develop more quickly; but I am well within the mark when I say that a tree cannot be expected to come into bearing in a period less than six to tern years. That is a long period. That is a long -wait, and these men who planted these orchards ten or fifteen years ago could not foresee the difficulties they were going to be confronted with, nor at that time did' this extreme production south of the line exist. I desire to say to the committee that the existence of this dumping clause and the fair and generous administration of it by the minister are absolutely essential to the livelihood of thousands of producers of fruit in the Okanagan and in other sections of western Canada as well as in eastern Canada.

The hon. member is all
right that far.

I want to draw attention to the fact that nobody in this House or, indeed, in Canada has fought against giving preference in trade where that would lessen protection, harder than the hon. member has himself.

My hon. friend is wrong
again.
At least, that is the impression I gather from the way in which he presents matters to the House.
I am sorry I apparently cannot make myself clear.

The people on the
prairie have no assurance that they are going to get their fruit for less by encouraging the people of the West Indies to go into raising citrus fruit to sell to them. If we put a tariff on that fruit, we know we shall have to pay more for it. That is what we oppose, and we cannot wait for citrus fruit or any other kind of fruit until they get their orchards going in that country. I want to see my hon. friend using logical arguments when he argues about protection to the fruit grower. I am quite willing that the man who is in the business should raise fruit in Canada for me to eat, and I want to eat it. But I do not want to be asked to wait for a new orchard to grow or to pay so much that I cannot afford to buy the fruit and, perhaps, soon be out of business and therefore not be able to buy any fruit at all.

Mr. Chairman, do you
not think we have considered this matter long enough-an hour and a half? Do you not think this House should attend to business.

As regards the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre that it was necessary to enforce the dumping clause in order to keep out United States fruit, and that the industry had been built up in that country by using similar tactics, I maintain that at the present time, our duty, without any dumping duty at all, is about the same as the duty which he calls a prohibitive duty on fruit going into the United States. The dumping clause was not

uniformly used ,to maintain the western market for British Columbia fruit because, at the very time it was used to keep fruit out of the prairies the city of Vancouver was importing Washington apples.
When did British Columbia import Washington apples?
Last August.

What quantity did British
Columbia import at that particular time?
I am not an encyclopedia. I do not know the quantity imported.
British Columbia has had a big surplus of apples and has never had any need to import any.

The hon. member for
Parkdale takes a good deal of exception to my statement that apples from Washington went into Vancouver. I heard him state this afternoon that he sometimes bought fruit from the United States. He frequently rises in his place and tells us just how we ought to conduct our business in the West. By the way, it may be of interest to call the attention of the committee to where Parkdale is. It represents as regards Toronto about the same position as a certain district does in regard to New York which George Ade made famous and possibly a little bit ridiculous in one of his songs:
Only forty-five minutes from Broadway
And nothing at all to do,
But stroll down to the depot
And see the trains go through.
I wish to call to the attention of the committee a telegram which was sent to the Growers Sales Agency from the British Columbia growers under date of August 24, 1923. There were several other telegrams preceding this one in which they had been ordering fruit from the growers and there had been some dispute. The growers did not wish to live up to the terms of the arrangement which they had previously made and they wanted to deliver a less quantity of fruit than they had previously agreed to deliver. This is the telegram and it also includes the price:
Regarding price Elbertas it was our understanding we were compelled meet competitors price from Washington and our idea in advising quantity was for purpose having you reserve sufficient outlet your market this quantity inasmuch as our fob quotations are always disregarded and it is impossible for us to get more than Washington is quoting, we cannot see advantage naming price until they ready move. We would, however, be satisfied with eighty-five cents fob Okanagan please advise as we do not want any more misunderstandings.

Supply-Customs
That is as far as I will read the telegram, There are three or four lines which are not germane to the subject. But you will notice in August last they were paying eighty-five cents for British Columbia apples and not somewhere around fifty or eighty cents as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre mentioned a short time ago.
I said the grower.

I do not understand the
statement. I presume if the grower got fifty or eighty cents, the jobber was paying it. This is a telegram to the growers from the dealers and most assuredly if the dealers are paying eighty cents, the jobbers are getting that, that is, f.o.b. Okanagan points, as quoted in the telegram. I want to reiterate that personally it is not with the intention in any way to hamper the fruit growing industry that I object to this dumping clause being administered. I think it manifestly unfair that the prairie provinces should be asked to pay for fruit a greater price than is charged in Vancouver when the grade is admittedly poor; and there is no justification for the anti-dumping clause to be introduced into the prairies to keep fruit out of that part of the country while fruit is being shipped into Vancouver city from Washington points.

Does the hon. member
know how much more the prairie man pays for the fruit in consequence of the application of the (anti-dumping clause? How much would he save if the clause were repealed? Many speeches are made about this matter but no one appears to know what the position is.

That has nothing to do
with the situation.
Suppose you paid one cent more, would you put these people out of business?

I would put the system
out of business whether I paid a cent or half a cent; the system is unjustifiable.
Mr. Chairman.-
That is not fair.

Will the minister give us a brief idea in regard to the expenditure of this money for preventive service? To what extent has that service been increased on the Pacific coast, and are aeroplanes being used now, and to what extent?

Supply-Customs

We are using aeroplanes to some extent on the Pacific coast but at no txpense to the department. The service on the Pacific coast is being improved both on the Pacific highway and at the coast; and we have now under consideration the construction of a number of fast motor boats to follow up smugglers of narcotics and liquors particularly. The Pacific coast has required a lot of additions owing to increased business and the great number of ships which now come into port as compared with previous years. The same thing applies on the Atlantic. We have had complaints that sufficient patrol was not exercised along the coast. There are various small harbours and islands along the Atlantic coast just as there are on the Pacific and they are very favourable to the smuggling enterprise.
How many cruisers are there?

.There is just one cruiser proper, the Margaret, which does service in the gulf of St. Lawrence and on the Atlantic coast. What particular class of goods are these smugglers bringing?
Liquor and narcotics.

I will agree to anything,

Mr. Chairman,
I understand there is a treaty or arrangement between Canada and the United States whereby pure bred live stock for breeding purposes is allowed to pass between the two countries free of duty. This arrangement is lived up to apparently, with one exception, which affects the province from which I come. The breeding of fur-bearing animals has now become a very large industry throughout the Dominion, particularly the breeding of silver black foxes in Prince Edward Island, which are registered by the National Records office the same as any other pure bred live stock. Our friends in the United States charge a duty of 15 per cent on such live stock, whereas they are allowed to bring their stock in here free of duty. If Canadians are compelled to pay this duty, it seems to me it is only fair that the Ameri-

Supply-Customs
cans should be treated in the same way or else they should recognize that silver blacik foxes are included in the arrangement referred to. I should like to hear from the minister in regard to tihis. I might also state that the fur trade between Canada and the United States has been very large. This question may not come under the present vote-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I have come to.
-but with your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring tihis to the attention of the committee.

All furs are
allowed into the States free of duty except silver black fox furs, on which a duty of 50 per cent is imposed, which is prohibitive. I have it from the Fur Merchants' Association in the United States, which is a very strong organization, that if representations were made by the Canadian government to Washington some relief could be obtained, the duty having been imposed at the request of a few American breeders. It may be thought that this does not affect Canada very much, but I would point out to the committee that it is a very serious matter. We have big fur auctions in Montreal every year, and these have been largely kept up by American buyers, who purchase silver fox furs and take them to the American side for sale or for shipment to the fur sales in London. The 50 per cent duty has practically prohibited the continuance of this practice. As a consequence the industry is hit very hard, and I am sure that if negotiations were taken up with the authorities at Washington some relief could be obtained. I refrain from discussing the matter further and will content myself by asking the minister if there is any treaty or arrangement with the United States regarding the interchange of pure-bred live stock.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry I cannot answer my friend, as this is a matter which would belong to the Department of Agriculture, and my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) will be in a better position to answer the question. The Department of Customs has nothing to do with such treaties except to collect whatever duties may be imposed.

Administration of the Migratory Birds Convention Act., $50,000.

Mr. Chairman, I do not
know whether the information I require should be asked for under this item, but can the minister tell me if there is any provision in his department for setting apart certain local areas for the protection of birds? I believe they are designated as bird sanctuaries.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior) :
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, throughout Canada there
are certain areas set apart for migratory and game birds where hunting is prohibited.

What protection is
afforded by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have
certain officers whose duty it is to administer the act in conjunction always with the local provincial game wardens. Most of the protection we get from these wardens. An agreement is usually made with the provincial authorities before the sanctuaries are established.
Are any of these sanctuaries situated in the prairie provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is the
list of bird sanctuaries:
Xova Scotia: Seal and Mud islands and vicinity.
Quebec: Bird rock, Bonaventure island, Perce rock.
Ontario: The provincial authorities of Ontario do not favour the creation of sanctuaries under the Migratory Birds Convention Act, in Ontario, claiming that the provincial law provides adequate protection.
There are no sanctuaries in Manitoba as yet; they are to be created. In Saskatchewan there are sanctuaries at Last Mountain lake, Indian Head nursery station, Sutherland nursery station, and eleven other sanctuaries are proposed as follows:
Johnson, Chaplin, Basin, Lenore, Big Stick, Crane, Manitou. Cabri, White Bear, Quill and Redberry lakes.
In Alberta we have sanctuaries at:
Many Islands, Pakowki, Birch, Buffalo, Miquelon, Ministik, La Biche, Rideau island and Calgary.
Supply-Interior

It is proposed to establish sanctuaries also at lake Newell and Bow River reservoir. In British Columbia we have sanctuaries at Vaseaux Lake and Victoria Harbour.
I would like very much if it had been possible to create a sanctuary for the Franklin gull in Manitoba. That is the gull that is a great destroyer of grasshoppers, and it does no one any harm.
Does this mean that -all birds are protected in the Indian Head nursery?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
I have seen crows there in thousands, so numerous that they are very destructive to fields of oats.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We do not protect crows, of course.
What birds are protected?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All the game birds, but crows are on the free list; you can shoot them op sight.
Why is there a reduction of $5,000 in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A considerable amount of the preliminary work has been done in connection with this vote, and we think we can get along with a little less. We could spend more money, it is true, but we have to economize wherever we can.
The work will not suffer as a result of this $5,000 reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, we hope as time goes on to get more assistance from provincial game wardens, who are under salary from the provincial governments.

I think it is generally appreciated that we should foster birds throughout the country. The dearth of birds has been considered the cause of many outbreaks of insects in the West, particularly in dry years. If we have lots of birds around it will minimize to a great extent the evils that come as a result of insects, and if an extra $5,000 would assist materially in bringing this work to a point where it would be of greater benefit, I would suggest that the item should not be reduced.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am very glad to hear my hon. friend say that, because in work of this kind, as in forestry and kindred matters where we are adopting preservative measures, it is purely a question of educating the public. I am receiving a large number of protests from people living 
in the vicinity of these sanctuaries, particularly in the settled areas, complaining that they are creating a weed nuisance and other evils. It is a matter of education, pure and simple.
Is there any co-operation between the provinces and the department in establishing these bird sanctuaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, yes.
I understand that Manitoba has an organization for this purpose at the present. Have they made application for assistance in any way?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We are
.working in co-operation with all the provinces, ,but some of them, Ontario for instance, have not thought it necessary as yet to establish bird sanctuaries, believing that the breeding is going on satisfactorily. To show you the interest that is taken in this matter, just recently on the marsh at Burlington, right near the city of Hamilton, we established a bird sanctuary. Interest is growing in this work, particularly in the settled areas. In the unsettled areas it is not so important, because there is plenty of protection. In Manitoba there is every evidence of interest.
Was there not a bird sanctuary created at Jack Miner's place in Essex county?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that is a provincial sanctuary.

A voluntary organization was established in Manitoba some two months ago, and I iwjught a membership card just prior to my departure for Ottawa. It is working independently of the provincial government altogether.
What sort of co-operation is there between the two governments in connection with the sanctuary at Hamilton?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Ontario,
owning its resources, works out the whole thing. We simply co-operate with them in protective measures. They are really in control. We cannot control the situation.
What is the nature of the co-operation of the federal government?

We carry on an educative propaganda, and try to assist any such organization as my hon. friend from Springfield has mentioned, and the provincial governments, in setting aside areas for the protection of wild life.

Supply-Interior
What obligation is there on this country with regard to the United States under the Migratoiy Birds Convention Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That will all be found in the Migratory Birds Convention Act. Each country undertakes protective measures, and takes responsibility for applying them. I might say, in passing, that it sometimes works a little hardship in the florth country where the natives have been in the habit of killing game birds when they return in the spring. Sometimes they are in rather desperate straits for food, but we are trying to the best of our ability to carry out our undertakings under that convention without creating hardship.

Around Toronto, right in the township of York, the lead that has been taken by the government in protecting wild birds has met with great success, and only last summer I saw very distinct evidence of that in the portion where I live. Not only was something being done by the government, but by the inhabitants of the township as well, by putting up bird retreats and bird houses, and the result is that you can hear any number of songsters there now that you could not hear years ago.
Is it obligatory under the convention for this country to provide sanctuaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that is one of the terms.
How do you manage to carry out that undertaking in provinces that have control of their own natural resources?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are under no obligation to enforce measures. It is well understood under the convention that we are to work in conjunotion with the provinces. We have no authority to go into any province owning its natural resources and compel the establishment of sanctuaries. We could do that in the three prairie provinces, but that is not the method we pursue. It is rather one of co-operation with the provinces, and it is of very great assistance to the department and the officials in charge to have voluntary associations working in conjunction with them.

There is a feeling in some sections of the country that the Americans take advantage of this treaty. It is claimed that early in the year when the birds are commencing to move north along the Atlantic coast the slaughter of birds is
permitted in United States territory up till, I think, the last day of February or some time in March. The people of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island feel that when they are prohibited from shooting birds at that season the same restriction should apply in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Of course
the main feature of the treaty is the prevention of the spring shooting when the birds are returning to their breeding ground. The Americans have undertaken that there should be no shooting in the United States after the 31st January.
That arrangement has been made lately.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is a provision of the treaty.

Item agreed to.
Engraving, lithographing, printing and preparation of maps, plans, reports and kindred publications of the Dominion, including salaries and necessary materials for same, etc., $137,495.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The increase here is due to three items. I may say that $7,770 is required for the work of two engineers who are engaged in field studies of development problems. Their purpose is to establish direct touch with business men, boards of trade and other commercial bodies who are in a position to give first hand information on resources that are available for new development, or on openings for sound industries based on Canadian raw materials. The total cost of this new work will exceed $12,000, but roughly speaking $5,000 of this additional expense is being met by economies in other directions such as in the consolidation of mapping work.
In the next place $3,000 is required for a new edition of " Canadh-Natural Resources and Commerce." This publication has met with an exceptional demand from banks, bond companies, and so forth, who through their British and American offices are directly engaged in attracting investment funds to the Dominion from abroad. It will be necessary very shortly to prepare a new English edition as well as to publish a French edition.
Then $6,025 is required to permit a start to be made on the publication of a loose-leaf economic atlas. The Atlas of Canada issued in 1915 is now obsolete in many respects. To revise and reprint it in its present form would cost about $45,000. By issuing loose-leaf form, the initial cost will be spread over several years and replacement costs thereafter will be reduced to the minimum.
Supply-Interior

These are the explanations for the items of increase. I may say that these are only items in the whole of these estimates in which there is an increase, the reason being that we are providing for the preparation of a very great number of maps, and also trying to bring to the attention of the investing funds both within the Dominion and outside as well, the possibilities for investment in Canadian resources. That is the object of the expenditure of this money. I have felt, notwithstanding the great need for economy, that I was warranted in asking parliament for a slight increase for this particular purpose, believing it will yield a very splendid return for the investment.
When does the minister expect to have the maps printed and ready for distribution?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is one other matter I neglected to mention. I propose to charge for some of these maps. We have not been doing so in the past to any great degree, but I believe that by doing so we will more than make up the increase in this item. The charge will be made with discretion. We are not going to exact it in the case of school districts, and municipalities. Sometimes, however we have a demand for one or two hundred of the maps to be used for semi-private purposes and in such cases we propose that a nominal fee shall be paid in order to take care of this work.
Some of the departmental reports are too bulky; they contain too much detail.

I am thoroughly in accord with the minister's proposition, but I hope that no legitimate request from any school section or any public body in Canada for a reasonable supply of these maps free of charge will be refused. In the past, school sections have always been supplied with maps when they asked for them, and I feel that the best way to get the youth of the country fully acquainted with the possibilities of Canada is by the circulation of these maps. Such a course, which is calculated to keep our young people at home when they arrive at maturity, is preferable to inducing foreigners to settle in Canada at the public expense. In my opinion one good Canadian is worth fifty foreigners brought in from outside.

$268,000 was collected!.

speechtext: That is a trust fund.

What was the cost of collecting the amount which was received last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

To collect $268,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. That is occasioned by the fact that we do a lot of work for which we get no return. We have to keep a staff. Does the minister send out collectors, or merely bill them?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
think we have any collectors in the field; we just bill them. We have our regular field officers, such as the homestead inspectors, who are once in a while instructed to visit these people and ascertain why we are not getting our money, and recommend, if necessary, drastic action.
Would it not be possible to collect these uncollected seed grain liens through the Soldier Settlement Board, and perhaps do it more efficiently?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think very much would be accomplished by sending the actual collectors out on the ground. I am rather opposed to any drastic action. Usually honest people will pay upon demand if they are able to pay; and if we find an individual from whom we cannot get any response, then the nearest homestead inspector will visit him and report upon his case. These claims all represent liens upon the land, and I think it would be a mistake to be too drastic in forcing collection.

I do not intend to
suggest taking drastic action in collecting the seed grain liens. I am quite aware of the fact that the people who owe the money to the government are usually not in a position to pay very much on their indebtedness, but the suggestion I made was that, instead of sending out homestead inspectors at; considerable cost, the staff of the Soldier Settlement Board might be utilized.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think the
suggestion is a good, one except for the fact that this is largely work done down here in our central office. The bookkeeping, and the billing and, everything in connection with it would all have to be done here. The: mere visiting of the individual who is delinquent is not required in very many cases. It is, however, in some cases; and in such cases our homestead inspector can do it. There would be no reason why the Soldier Settlement official could not do it, except that he would not be very familiar with that particular work.
Could the minister tell how much is outstanding now?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the three provinces we have outstanding on principal $3,751,775, and on interest $1,504,996.44, or a total of $5,256,771.44. The $3,000,000 unpaid is the remaining amount of the $18,000,000 advanced.	*

What is the rate of
interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Six per cent is the ordinary rate, and on an overdue account seven per cent.
Is $50,000 the full amount now in arrears?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh no. I just gave the amount, $5,000,000 odd.

Is that the full amount in
arrears?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that is all in arrears. There have been no issues recently, so that it is all in arrears just now.

What is the total amount
unpaid?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The amounts are $3,751,775 of principal, and $1,504,996.44 of interest, making a total of $5,256,771.44.

The item in the estimates
reads:
Seed grain advances-amount required to meet uncollected portions of advances of seed grain made in the western provinces by the chartered banks to holders of unpatented Dominion lands under the guarantee of the Dominion government; also for clerical assistance, travelling expenses, etc., $50,000.
How is it you can get rid of a liability such as the minister has mentioned by providing $50,000, if it is all overdue?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This amount is only for the purpose of paying our staff engaged on this work. I might explain that
Supply-Interior

after the item was drafted we changed the wording but when estimates were sent over to the Finance department, through an oversight, they did not adopt our new wording, and it is somewhat ambiguous. This is merely payment for the service of the staff.

I would say it is more than
ambiguous. It is absolutely wrong. I am not offering any criticism. It says that it is "to meet uncollected portions of advances", and that is not so. It is just for clerical services and travelling expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We ask
for $50,000 as an amount required to pay the expenses connected with seed grain and relief collections. They did not adopt that wording, and we did not notice the difference in the wording.

I think possibly just a little injustice is done by this department to some of the municipalities and to some of the village councils. The minister said a moment ago that the security of the seed grain liens was upon land, but in some instances, when the grain was advanced to farmers, they also put in as security village lots. Since that time a good many of the farmers have not been able to pay their taxes upon the village lots, with the result that the village lots have been bought by the villages at the tax sales. Now as a result of the seed grain lien still being held upon these lands, they are unable to get title, and are just as badly off as they were before. They bought the lots and I understand application has been made to the minister to release the seed grain liens upon village property, so that the village councils can sell the lots and get the results of the tax sales. But so far there has been no relief, and I ask the minister if he could not give relief to municipalities under those circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am informed that in 1915 when the last redistribution was made, an individual who happened to own village property as well as his farm land, had all the property owned by him placed under the lien. This is something new to me, but I am advised that in many cases where we have ample security on the farm lands, the village property has been released. As my hon. friend well knows, it is not a very good thing to release security until the debt is paid. We have endeavoured to meet legitimate requests for relief where we, of course, are protected ourselves, because we would be subject to a great deal of criticism if we released security and took chances of a loss.

Wherever an individual has farm lands upon which a lien was placed, there would be no objection to releasing the village property provided that the farm land afforded ample security.

The instances I could cite are these, that the farmer left the land, left the district. He possibly made a small payment on the village lot and then it was put up for sale to meet unpaid taxes. No one bought it, so the village bought it in in order to resell it and it cannot get title to the property until the seed grain lien is removed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
None of
those cases has been brought to my attention. I would be glad to deal with each of them that might be brought up, upon its merits.

Item agreed to.
To cover defalcation of A. C. Oxley, seed grain collector, for amount paid to him by Jacob Schneider in November, 1917, 1334.55.
Will the minister explain this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is a
case in which a collector named Oxley received from Jacob Schneider $334.55 as payment for seed grain indebtedness against a certain quarter section. He issued the subagent of Dominion lands' receipt for the money, but the money was never received by the department. Oxley was guaranteed by the Ocean and Accident Company for $3,000. His bond was cancelled on November 8, 1918; that is before we discovered the defalcation. In order to clear the land with the treasury, we have to issue the official receipt and we require this appropriation. We must vote this money.
Have proceedings been taken against Oxley?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is out of the country and we have been unable to locate him.

The defalcation happened before the bond was cancelled. The company must be responsible for the amount even if the defalcation was not detected until the bond was released.
Mr.'STEWART (Argenteuil): The difficulty in this particular case was this. We find in western Canada that even transfers take place with seed grain liens attached. I know of one particular case in my locality which occurred before I came to Ottawa, in which a transfer had taken place and an innocent man was billed for the lien against property that he had purchased from an individual who moved

Supply-Interior
out of the country and went to the United States. A great deal of difficulty was experienced' in straightening that out. This was a case in which the man collected the money, made no return, and his bond had expired before the defalcation was discovered. When we billed Schneider we found that he had paid the money to Oxley and had his receipt. In the meantime Oxley was out of the country, the guarantee company's bond had expired and we had no recourse against the company. It might be inferred that some official should be made to account for this, but it can very easily happen. The only notification we get is when we bill the individual for the money, and in many cases, as my hon. friends who live on farms know, we get no response. This is a case that has happened just in that way.
Was the defalcation made during the life-time of the bond?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I imagine it was.
Why would the company not be responsible?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This happened in 1917, long before my day. I cannot tell the committee why action was not taken against the company, but I doubt if action could be sustained against the company after the expiry of the bond when no demand was made. My hon. friend will know that better than I.

I quite agree that it would depend on the wording of the bond no doubt but it struck me that, merely because the bond had expired, that might not be sufficient. This, however, is not a very large item and I will not detain the committee.

When did the department
discover the defalcation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Four years afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am told
that Schneider was billed repeatedly, but never responded, so that the defalcation could not be discovered until he produced the receipt, naturally the assumption in the department being that Schneider owed the money.

Item agreed to.
Amount required to provide relief by way of necessary supplies of food, clothing, fuel, etc., also fodder for animals, to needy settlers of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan by co-operation and agreement with the provincial governments or otherwise, and under regulations to be made by the Governor in Council, $100,000.

Somewhat similar conditions have existed in the northern part of New Ontario during the past few years and there was considerable distress which required emergency relief. I would urge upon the government that the principle of this appropriation should be extended from Alberta and Saskatchewan to New Ontario where a good deal of emergency relief is required and the provincial goverment have been responsible for it. New Ontario is a district which has been very much overlooked by this legislature. For example, the government of Ontario have to build their own provincial railway from the Transcontinental up to James bay. This legislature would not give them a grant. In Manitoba this was built by the government of Canada. I am not opposing this grant because no doubt this relief is badly needed and the money is wisely and well expended, but some consideration should be given as regards similar conditions of emergency relief in the northern district of New Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It would be well to recite how this comes about. This is not a direct obligation of the federal government. As my hon. friend knows, in Ontario all the resources are owned by the provincial government. In western Canada the resources are owmed by the federal government. This sum represents really 50 per cent of the loss sustained. These obligations were incurred by the municipalities, the municipalities obligating themselves in the first instance. A secondary obligation was by the provincial government, and then an arrangement was entered into between the provincial government and the federal government that where the money was borrowed by the municipalities from the banks and where the municipalities were unable to collect and the banks refused to carry the loan longer, the two governments became liable for 50 per cent of the losses.
That does not mean that the money or some portion of it will not be collected eventually. The two governments are responsible on a 50 per cent basis for the amount that cannot be collected, and the only liability the federal government is assuming is a half responsibility with the province for such sums as might not be collected by the banks who loaned the money to the municipalities in the first instance.

I see no difference between the situation as stated by my hon. friend (Mr. Church) and such a situation as might occur in any province where the Dominion owns the land. It is a matter of distress in any event, and I see no reason why the government should assume responsibility for a situation of that kind in Alberta and not in Ontario. As pointed out by my hon. friend, the Ontario government has largely come to the relief of settlers in parts of the province where they are exposed to exactly the same dangers and where they have had in the past at least, precisely the same difficulties, and probably in many instances greater difficulties than have ever been experienced in any of the provinces mentioned by the minister.

Last fall the Lieutenant Governor of this province, as well as the premier of the province and the Hon. Dr. Cody, former Minister of Education, went over the James bay district. They came in contact with untold distress and witnessed many hardships in that vast hinterland of Ontario where the people are cut off from all communication in the winter. The district is inaccessible, there is hardly any medical attendance which the people can fall back upon, and there are no modem appliances of any kind; but the government of Ontario is doing its part to relieve the situation. And similar conditions exist in northern Ontario. I am not objecting to anything being done for either Alberta or Saskatchewan, but I do urge the minister to consider favourably the case for those settlers in Ontario who are in need of relief. We have in northern Ontario a vast new country which has been left to shift for itself, and no one will settle there. The early settlers in that part of the province faced many privations and they are to-day denied the conveniences which the people in well favoured parts of the Dominion enjoy.
If the Venerable Archdeacon Cody visited the district on a government delegation what was his report?

I am just asking the minister to let us have equality of treatment for all the provinces in these votes, whidh are supposed to be for the general advantage of Canada and not for the good of any particular province. When one province is given the benefit of the vote, any other .province in which equally deserving conditions exist should be given the same treatment. If there are circumstances that call for relief in Nova Scotia that province is entitled to that relief just as much as the others.
I was not complaining.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The conditions are not identical as between Ontario and the West. The federal government owns all the lands in western Canada; the provinces do not own a foot of them. The lands in that part of the Dominion come under the jurisdiction of the provinces only when they pass into private hands, and the federal government to-day is getting a revenue from those lands which it is not receiving from Ontario.

After the lands are preempted, when they come under the control of the settler in the West, the Dominion government has no more control over them than it has in northern Ontario. So that the situations are exactly similar.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. In Ontario all your mines are owned by the provincial government; and the forests all belong to the province. That is not the case in the West.
Are the mines in the West not owned by the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, by the federal government.
All?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Those that have not passed out of our control by sale or otherwise.
As I undertsand it, this vote is for the relief of distress in certain provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend has not caught my meaning at all. The situation in Ontario is so dissimilar from that in the West that I cannot understand why there should be any controversy on the matter.
Is this vote, or is it not, for the relief of distress in certain provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it is for relief of distress, that is true; but the federal government owns the land in the West.
That makes no difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, well, if it makes no difference I have no argument, I am through. What I was going to say was that as the federal government had an interest in the West, inasmuch as it owned the land, it should go to the rescue of those people. In this case it has not done so.

Then why the vote of
last year?

Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
For this
reason. The municipalities took upon themselves the responsibility for any losses that might occur, and as the federal government was an interested party we divided the responsibility between the provincial and the federal authorities.

The minister cannot get
away from the fact that when these lands are alienated from the Crown and come into the possession of the settler they are no longer under the control of the federal government.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is
true.

Therefore they are in
exactly the same position as the lands occupied by settlers in any other province in which the province owns the land. This vote is to provide relief by way of necessary supplies of food, clothing, fuel, and so on, for certain settlers; and as the situation in Ontario is identically the same as that in western Canada there is no reason why the same relief should not be given in the former province.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend must not forget that the homesteaders are included in this list-
That may be.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: -and they are on property that may revert to the federal government.

That does not alter the
federal government's position in the slightest. The fact of the matter is that this is really a vote for the relief of the municipalities and not for the settlers; it is for the relief of the provincial governments and the municipalities concerned.

When was this agreement made with the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, what is the nature of the agreement, and how long is it to continue? Further, how much are the provincial governments contributing per annum?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The agreement was made in 1920.

Perhaps I can throw
some light on the situation, having been at one time associated with municipal life in Alberta. The federal government gave no assistance to such settlers as held the title to the land they occupied; any assistance it gave to needy settlers was given to those who were on lands held by the Crown. Owing
to the fact that the provincial governments could not pass any regulations whereby the municipalities Could place a lien against the land belonging to the Crown, it became necessary for the federal government to step in and offer some assistance. I can assure the committee that all this assistance was given to people who occupied Crown lands and consequently it was not incumbent upon the provincial governments to come to their aid.

Would this apply to the
Peace river block where 3,500,000 acres of land are owned by the Dominion government?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It applies
wherever the Dominion government owns any land.

It would therefore apply
to the Peace river block?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Can the minister give
us any information regarding the agreement between the two governments? The language of this vote is very comprehensive; it speaks of lan agreement
-with the provincial governments or otherwise.

What is the significance
of the phrase "or otherwise"?
It leaves the matter very wide open.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, I was the individual who made the agreement in the first place. The plea I made upon that occasion was the plea I make to-night.
Why "or otherwise?"

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The wording is somewhat ambiguous, but I hope you will not hold me responsible for all the wording here. There is an agreement between the provincial governments and the federal government. I might read the order in council, but it does not throw any light on the agreement. Briefly, the agreement provides that where relief is needed in the province the money is borrowed from the banks and guaranteed-
By whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
By the municipality in most cases; by the province itself where the territory is not organized. Both the municipality and the province borrow money from the bank and accept responsibility for the administration. The federal authorities come in where there is inability to collect
Supply-Interior

loans and the banks refuse to carry the accounts any longer. That does not mean the security upon the land is cancelled. The two governments agree within a reasonable time to recompense the banks in cases where overdue accounts are carried too long. We accept the statement of the provincial government that there is, say, $25,000 to be repaid to the banks, and we pay half and the province pays the other half. It is hoped that eventually this money will be collected. That, in a nutshell, is the agreement.
When was the agreement made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In 1920. It is renewed year by year.

been made by the federal government on account of the agreement?
