Mr. McQUAlRRIE: Has any of this money been repaid to the government of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The province of Alberta has repaid up to date $46,090.23, and Saskatchewan $15,336.62, or a total of $61,426.85.

What efforts are being made to get this money back? For instance, are you taking the same procedure as

in the case of loans to returned soldiers. These men, I understand, are being continually asked for repayment and threatened with all kinds of dire consequences should thej fail to pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We do not
collect this money; the provincial authorities have that responsibility.
What are they doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are
trjdng to collect it,
In what manner?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend particulars.
Does not the minister think he should find out whether the provincial governments are endeavouring to get the money back?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They tell us they are.
What do they say they are doing?
Oh, oh.

I think that is a fair question and not a joke. I know it does not seem to be a joke so far as the returned soldier is concerned. I should think it would be the business of the minister to find out what the provincial governments are doing to get back this money. It is hardly sufficient to say, "Well, the provincial governments say they are doing something." We do not know what they are doing. Has the minister made any serious effort to find out what steps the provincial governments are taking to get this money back?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend knows that the provincial governments are responsible for the collection. They report to us every three months what collections they have made. I have not inquired as to what methods the provincial authorities are pursuing, and therefore cannot give my hon. friend the information that he asks for. As to the returned soldiers, please do not blame me; I have nothing to do with the collection of the loans made to them.

Mr. Chairman, I have every sympathy with the settler in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and I have no doubt that at the time this agreement was made such help was absolutely necessary. But four years have elapsed and this grant is going on from year to year. In other provinces, in northern Ontario and northern Quebec, for

Supply-Interior
instance, men are in such circumstances, due to no fault of their own, that they should receive the same treatment. I cannot see why we should not have organizations in those provinces doing similar work. The mere fact that the land in the western provinces is under federal control does not seem to me to make any difference in the circumstances. I would suggest to the minister that he discontinue this grant, or find out why it should be continued from year to year.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are not continuing it.

You are, apparently, by
this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not correct.

There is a vote of $100,000, and there is already, according to the minister's own figures, $750,000 outstanding. It is continued from year to year. At the same time the settlers in the other provinces have no provision made for relief of this kind.

I have heard the
word "resources" used quite a bit, and for my own information I would ask what resources has the Dominion in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
All the
crown lands and all the timber which has not passed into the hands of private ownership, and all minerals of every character.

As soon as they pass
into private hands-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a different thing.

That is different.
When land passes into the hands of the settler, all the resources in connection with it go too?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

And they pass
then to the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not the
mineral resources, since '98.

The land passes
to the individual, and it is then an asset of the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.

So what the Dominion did was to pay a certain amount of
money to the Hudson's Bay Company for the purchase of the land, and the guarantee and obligation for that money fell on the older provinces. There were practically no settlers in these districts except a few brought in by the Hudson's Bay Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is perfectly right. The individual who lives in the Northwest Territories helps to pay his share of the purchase price just the same as the individual living in the older provinces.
So that we can understand the situation, when was that debt actually paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not the date with me.
In 1904, I think.
What does the minister mean by saying minerals have not passed since '98?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The minerals did not go with the grants; they remained the property of -the federal government.
That is only surface rights have passed since '98 to the settlers, but the policy as to releasing instead of selling mineral rights was inaugurated in 1913.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What I mean is that since '98 the crown grant did not carry the mineral rights with it.
On the general question of the natural resources-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Don't bring that up now.
I suppose that is as near a solution as it was a year ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not give my hon. friend any further information than was given a year ago.

I think that is about
right. It is just where is was a year ago, and two years ago. It is just where it was at the time of the housetop pronouncement that a solution had been found for that question. That was about two years and four months ago, and the solution is still on the housetop.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This question of the natural resources is bound to be a matter of very great controversy, and I think my hon. friend knows that as well as anyone.

I never announced a solution.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is very discreet.

I hope the minister will
underline that remark of his in Hansard and hand it to the Prime Minister to-morrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think he understands that.
He ought to; he has had enough lessons.

I would like to ask a question of the minister with reference to a communication I received recently from southern Alberta, where in certain parts of the province the land is of such a quality that it is almost impossible for the settlers to make a living and stay there. In the first place the Dominion was responsible for bringing these settlers on to that land. These settlers have spent the last ten or fifteen years of their fives there trying to make a living on that land, and the communication I received asked if there was any possibility of the government coming to their assistance by paying the transportation expenses of their moving out, that is, taking their stock and implements to some other part of the province where they could start operations on land that might possibly yield them a living. I put that before the minister and would ask him if there is any possibility of giving assistance to these settlers. I would call the attention of the House to this important fact:	So far as the province is concerned, they have no responsibility at all, for these settlers went in there at the direction of the Dominion authorities, and we maintain that to all intents and purposes the federal government is responsible for settling them on this land on which they cannot make a living.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
For a period of two or three years there was a sum of money granted by the provincial and federal authorities for moving these settlers out, but no request has come to me officially within the past two years for a continuation of the grant. There was an attempt made to make it possible for these people to take up new homesteads in the northern portion of the province, and some assistance was given, but not to any very great extent. Like many other problems it is very difficult to work out.

That was the report to me of the Minister of Agriculture from the province of Alberta, and as I say, I have not been notified by the provincial authorities that there was any further interest in that direction.

The information I received did not. come from the provincial authorities, but direct from the settlers themselves. I should like to know if the minister would be inclined to favour such a proposal again. I would point out to the House this very important point, that we are spending millions of dollars each year to bring people in here from other countries. Now we have brought here these settlers of whom I speak and they are settled on land they cannot make a living upon, and I ask would it not be better for this parliament to vote money to aid these settlers already on the land, who are experienced and are of much more value to Canada than the new settlers we are spending millions of dollars each year to bring in. I think some effort should be made at least to pay or assist in paying the transportation expenses of these settlers, so that they can move somewhere else where they can rent or buy land and start fife over again. I think the money would be well spent, even if it was taken out of the immigration estimates. I think it would be better spent in that way' than in bringing in the people we are getting at the present time.

Is there any portion of
this amount for the relief of returned soldiers, or is that chargeable to the Soldier Settlement Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
think any portion of this would be for returned soldiers, because that is an obligation directly of the Soldier Settlement Board and the federal government. I would not like to be absolutely definite on that point.

Is there no obligation
on the part of the provincial governments to return this money to the Dominion government, provided they do not collect from individual settlers? Is there not a term in the agreement that compels that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The agreement provides for our half of the advance upon collection, but there is no obligation on the part of the provincial government to return the money if they cannot collect it. But as I pointed out, all these advances are made upon the security of land, and the obligation remains against the land.

Does the minister say the agreement of 1920 bound the government for 1924-25?
Mr., STEWART (Argenteuil):	No, only
for one year.
Only for one year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Just for one
year.

The piinister simply
found the terms fair, and has carried them on year after year himself since?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that is correct.

It is a pity we have
not decided some other things. May I ask what is the present condition of the immortal, the historic Hoppe leases? Are they still reserved or has the government done any bedevilling in that situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think hon. members will recollect that last year the Hoppe leases were put under control of parliament.
They are still there?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
know how they would get away.

I have heard rumours,
that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Oh, yes, I
have heard those too. I believe our names are connected in rumours of that character.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is still an item
of $8,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That stands at the request of the ex-Minister of Finance. It has to do with the Chicago drainage matter and I prefer to let it stand until the hon. member is in his seat.

May I ask if the $1,000
vote to the Alpine Club went through without any protest from the member for La-prairie and Napierville (Mr. Lanctot) and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster)?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Without any question.

In regard to the vote
of $8,000-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
That has not been
called; it stands.

I know it is standing
in order that the return of correspondence may be seen by the ex-Minister of Finance. I made inquiry last night in regard to the matter and the minister's secretary stated we would get it to-day. I should like to have the fde so as to go through it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The file is
here and contains the correspondence with the exception of a despatch to which we have not had a reply.

I have been trying
to get it and have not been able to locate it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My recollection is that the Prime Minister placed the file in the custody of the Clerk of the House There is, as I pointed out to the committee, one despatch that has not been brought down for the reason that we have not had a reply to it.

The correspondence
brought down that I saw was only up to a long time ago. It was not a bit of value at all-much like nearly all that is brought down, sketchy and patchy. I do not know that it was patchy up to t'he time it ceased, but it ceased long ago. The correspondence brought down is certainly not up to date in connection with the Chicago drainage canal

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I had something to do with looking into the correspondence before it was brought down and the officers concerned were instructed to include in the return everything except two despatches. There are not more than two- perhaps only one-that have not been brought down. If they were not included in the return it is not the intention of the department to withhold them.
Has the government communicated with the British authorities on this subject?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister has informed the right hon. leader of the opposition as to that. The item is to stand; it is not to be debated to-night.
We should like to have all the correspondence bearing on the subject.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This item has not
been called. It is not proper to discuss it at present, it still stands for debate.
Crowsnest Pass Agreement

The country is far from
satisfied that the government have taken a proper attitude in this matter. It is pretty nearly time they did take a firm stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I again remind the
hon. gentleman that the item has not been called. Is it intended to proceed further in committee of Supply?

I think we have done
very well to-night.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does the right hon .gentleman not wish to go on?

I think we have done
very well. We have got through with the estimates of two departments practically.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 11.10 p.m.
